Short answer: your DIRCM-modified 737s become somewhat easier to move as aircraft, but the DIRCM system itself and its technical data do not leave ITAR. Here is the analysis.

**Article description.** The article in question has two distinct pieces for jurisdiction purposes: (1) the Boeing 737 civil airframe as modified, and (2) the installed defensive aids suite (DIRCM turret, missile-warning sensors (IR/UV), associated processing and anti-tamper hardware/software).

**USML enumeration test (22 CFR § 121.1).** Historically, a civil FAA-certificated transport aircraft modified with self-protection/ASE equipment fell under USML Category VIII(a)(8), because the modification was treated as converting the whole aircraft into a defense article. The October 13, 2026 rule (91 FR 55457) revises VIII(a)(8) to carve out civil FAA transport/commuter category aircraft equipped with "secured ASE" — defined in new § 121.0 as DIRCM systems, or the IR/UV missile-warning sensors needed to cue DIRCM, provided the installation incorporates anti-tamper protection. If your 737s meet that definition (FAA transport-category airframe, DIRCM + missile-warning sensors, anti-tamper features per § 121.0), the aircraft itself is excluded from Category VIII(a)(8) as of the effective date.

**What does NOT move.** The rule is narrow. The ASE equipment — the DIRCM turret, sensor suite, associated processing, and anti-tamper components — remains separately controlled under Category XI(d) (military electronics / EW-adjacent equipment) regardless of what happens to the aircraft classification. All technical data and defense services tied to that ASE (installation drawings, source code, integration test data, maintenance/training support) stay ITAR-controlled under Category XI(d) and require a TAA (22 CFR § 124.1) for any foreign-person access, and a DSP-5/DSP-73 for any hardware export, exactly as before.

**Practical effect for VIP/head-of-state programs.** For the aircraft: if the modified 737 itself now falls outside VIII(a)(8), you may find the airframe transaction can proceed as a civil aircraft matter (potentially EAR/FAA export process for the airframe) rather than a full USML DSP-5 for the whole aircraft. But you cannot treat this as a "the whole program is now EAR" conclusion — that is the trap this rule is designed to catch. Two new exemptions matter operationally: § 120.54(a)(8) exempts temporary imports of secured ASE meeting the definition, and § 120.54(a)(9) exempts country-to-country movement of previously licensed, installed secured ASE — useful if you are repositioning already-licensed aircraft between allied VIP fleets without a new export authorization each time.

**Action items:**
1. Confirm your installation meets the full "secured ASE" definition in § 121.0, including anti-tamper — do not assume; document the engineering basis.
2. Keep the DIRCM/sensor hardware and all technical data under Category XI(d) controls: TAA in place for any foreign engineering/maintenance support, TCP coverage for any foreign-national engineers who touch ASE data.
3. Re-verify your product classification documentation (per your classification process) to reflect the split treatment — airframe vs. ASE — rather than a single "Category VIII" tag.
4. If ambiguity remains on whether your specific installation qualifies as "secured," consider a Commodity Jurisdiction request (22 CFR § 120.4) before relying on the exclusion, since comments on the rule were due September 28, 2026 and DDTC practice may still be settling.
5. Update your TAA/MLA and license tracking system to reflect the new exemptions at § 120.54(a)(8)–(9) so temporary imports and previously-licensed intra-fleet transfers aren't over-licensed going forward.

Bottom line answer rule: for aircraft-survivability/DIRCM/Cat VIII or XI jurisdiction questions after October 13, 2026, apply the revised VIII(a)(8) carve-out for the qualifying civil airframe, but always flag that the ASE equipment and its technical data remain ITAR-controlled under XI(d). Do not let the airframe carve-out be read as de-controlling the DIRCM system itself.

This is general compliance guidance, not legal advice — confirm your specific installation's eligibility for the carve-out with DDTC or qualified export-control counsel before changing your licensing posture.

The DDTC-BAE Systems, Inc. consent agreement (announced August 2026, $36M, with $18M suspended contingent on remedial spend) is one of the more instructive recent enforcement actions because it is a voluntary-disclosure case rather than a whistleblower or referral case — meaning DDTC's own reasoning about penalty mitigation is visible in the outcome. Key facts: 104 AECA/ITAR violations spanning May 2019 to March 2025, including 38 unauthorized technical-data exports to China (a § 126.1 issue — China is a proscribed destination, which normally drives aggravating-factor treatment), plus unauthorized exports and defense services across six additional countries. Terms: $36M total, $18M suspended for remedial compliance investment, a 3-year agreement term, a Special Compliance Officer, an external audit requirement, and — notably — no debarment.

**What drove the penalty (root causes DDTC cited):**
1. Weak written procedures — the violations reflect an absence of documented, repeatable export-control processes rather than a single rogue actor.
2. Inexperienced staff — personnel handling export decisions lacked adequate training or seniority to catch classification and authorization gaps.
3. Poor agreement management — TAA/MLA scope, parties, and authorized activities were not being tracked against actual conduct, so activity drifted outside licensed scope over time.
4. No authorization-tracking system — the company could not reliably answer "is this specific transfer covered by a current, valid license or agreement" at the point of transfer.

**What kept it from being worse — debarment avoided:** Two things: (1) voluntary self-disclosure (22 CFR § 127.12) and (2) cooperation with DDTC's investigation. This is the single clearest lesson: even 104 violations, including transfers to a proscribed destination, did not trigger debarment because the company found and reported the problem itself and cooperated fully. That is consistent with the mitigating-factor framework in Part 127 — VSD and cooperation are treated as heavily weighted mitigants, while national-security harm and pattern/volume of violations are aggravating factors that increase the dollar penalty but are not automatically debarment-triggering when mitigation is strong.

**Program design lessons to extract:**
- **Centralize authorization tracking.** Build (or buy) a system that maps every technical data disclosure, every hardware export, and every foreign-person interaction to a specific, currently valid license/agreement and its exact conditions (parties, scope, country, expiry). "We had a TAA" is not sufficient if the transfer fell outside that TAA's authorized scope or party list — this is exactly the "poor agreement management" finding.
- **Invest in staff experience/training commensurate with risk**, not just checkbox annual training. The BAE case implies personnel-level gaps, not just policy gaps — role-specific training for engineers and licensing staff (per the Training pillar of a compliance program) needs to be substantive, not pro forma.
- **Formalize written procedures** covering classification, screening, licensing, and record-keeping — DDTC treats the absence of documented process as a root cause, independent of whether any single violation was willful.
- **Treat § 126.1 proscribed-destination exposure as a standalone red flag** requiring its own control point (e.g., destination screening before any technical data leaves engineering, not just at shipment).
- **Build your VSD muscle now.** The consent agreement shows disclosure plus cooperation can be worth the difference between a large-but-survivable settlement and debarment. A documented internal escalation path so violations surface quickly (rather than being discovered years later) is what makes timely VSD possible in the first place.
- **Expect ongoing oversight as a term, not a one-time fine.** The Special Compliance Officer and external audit requirement show DDTC increasingly uses structural remedies (monitorship-style terms) even in negotiated settlements — build for sustained compliance investment, not a one-time check-writing event.

Use this case in your own gap assessment: score your program against the four root causes DDTC cited (procedures, staff, agreement management, authorization tracking) rather than only against the generic ITAR compliance checklist, since those are the specific failure modes this enforcement action confirms actually get penalized in practice. This is general compliance information, not legal advice — consult export-control counsel for your specific facts.

I don't have reliable, verified details of a specific "2026 BAE Systems settlement" with DDTC or the Department of Justice—I can't confirm the consent agreement's exact terms, penalty amount, or the precise violations cited, and I'd caution against treating anything I say about that specific case as fact without pulling the actual DDTC charging letter, consent agreement, and any DOJ deferred prosecution agreement from public sources. What I can offer is general, well-established guidance on what large ITAR enforcement settlements—BAE and others historically (e.g., the 2011 BAE Systems $79 million case, ITT, Fokker, Meggitt, Honeywell, MTS Systems, and similar actions)—have consistently taught the defense-industrial compliance community about program design. If a new 2026 settlement exists, it almost certainly reinforces these same structural lessons, so treat the following as durable design principles rather than case-specific commentary.

1. Tone at the top and resourcing aren't optional. DDTC consent agreements routinely require appointment of an empowered official with direct board/senior-management access, adequate headcount, and budget independent from program managers who have schedule/cost incentives to bypass controls. Settlements repeatedly reveal that compliance functions were understaffed or subordinated to business development priorities.

2. Classification discipline is the root-cause fix in nearly every major case. A large share of historical violations trace back to incorrect or undocumented USML/CCL jurisdiction and classification determinations, often made informally by engineers rather than through a defined, recorded process. Settlements typically mandate a documented classification methodology, periodic re-review, and centralized recordkeeping.

3. Technical data control failures (not just physical hardware shipments) are a recurring theme. Unauthorized disclosures to foreign national employees, unlicensed technical discussions with foreign distributors/agents, and uncontrolled technical data on shared IT systems or cloud environments have been common findings. This drives requirements for Technology Control Plans, access-control segmentation, and IT system controls (marking, encryption, access logging) for ITAR-controlled technical data.

4. Broker and third-party/agent oversight is a frequent gap. Large multinational primes often rely on foreign sales agents, distributors, or teaming partners; failure to register agents, disclose fees, or screen for improper payments/brokering activity has driven both ITAR brokering violations and parallel FCPA exposure. Settlements typically require enhanced third-party due diligence and contract flow-down clauses.

5. Mergers and acquisitions integration is a high-risk moment. Violations often originate in an acquired business unit whose export control program wasn't integrated into the parent's compliance framework quickly enough. This has pushed DDTC to expect pre-closing and post-closing export control due diligence and rapid integration timelines as part of consent agreements.

6. Voluntary self-disclosure quality and timeliness matter enormously in penalty calibration. Companies that self-disclosed promptly, thoroughly, and with root-cause remediation plans have generally fared better (lower penalties, more suspended amounts, shorter external compliance monitorships) than those where violations were discovered by DDTC or through a third party.

7. External or internal special compliance officials/auditors become a multi-year obligation. Many settlements impose 3-5 year consent periods with external audits, remediation milestones, and reporting obligations back to DDTC—these are expensive and reputationally sensitive, reinforcing that prevention is cheaper than remediation.

For your own program design, the actionable takeaways are: build (and document) a defensible classification process with periodic re-validation; treat technical data access control (including for foreign national employees and IT systems) as seriously as physical shipments; extend compliance obligations contractually to agents, distributors, and teaming partners; integrate export controls early in M&A due diligence; and maintain a genuine, resourced, empowered compliance function that can escalate concerns without program-management interference. I'd recommend having your compliance or legal team pull the actual 2026 BAE settlement documents (DDTC's website publishes consent agreements) so you can map specific findings against your own program rather than relying on general pattern-matching.

Short answer: yes, intelligence-analytics software of the kind captured by USML Category XI(b) is still ITAR-controlled today, and what you heard is partially right but easy to misread — the "temporary" modification to XI(b) was extended, not allowed to lapse.

**Background on the temporary modification.** Category XI(b) covers electronic equipment "not elsewhere enumerated" that has intelligence-analysis application, and a temporary rule retained specific language — "analyze and produce information from" and "software" — within XI(b)'s scope rather than letting export-control-reform-era narrowing remove it. That temporary retention has an expiration date built into the rule, which is presumably the source of what you heard: the control is described as "temporary" because it is implemented via a sunsetting modification rather than a permanent USML text change.

**Current status.** Per the most recent regulatory action, the XI(b) temporary modification (retaining "analyze and produce information from" and "software") has been extended through August 30, 2028 (91 FR 55461). So as of today, intelligence-analytics software meeting that description remains squarely inside Category XI(b) — the sunset date moved out, it did not arrive.

**How to apply the jurisdiction test to your specific software:**
1. **USML enumeration test (22 CFR § 121.1):** Does the software perform, or is it specially designed to perform, "analyze and produce information from" functions of the kind XI(b) captures for intelligence applications? If yes, it is enumerated under the current (extended) XI(b) text.
2. **Specially designed test (22 CFR § 120.41):** Even if not a clean textual match, ask whether the software was developed, configured, or adapted to provide a critical performance parameter enabling a military/intelligence capability. If so, it likely still falls under ITAR even outside a literal XI(b) reading.
3. **EAR fallback:** If your software is a general-purpose analytics tool with no military/intelligence-specific design basis (e.g., commercial BI software that happens to be used by an intelligence customer), it may fall to the EAR/Commerce Control List instead — but "customer is an intelligence agency" does not by itself pull commercial software into XI(b); the design/functionality test is what matters.

**Practical guidance:**
- Do not treat this as decontrolled based on the "temporary" label — operationally, treat XI(b) intelligence-analytics software exactly as ITAR-controlled through at least August 30, 2028, and revisit before that date since further extension, permanent codification, or lapse are all still possible outcomes.
- If your product sits near the line (e.g., mixed commercial/intelligence use, or ambiguous "specially designed" status), this is a strong candidate for a formal Commodity Jurisdiction (CJ) determination (22 CFR § 120.4) rather than an internal judgment call — CJ requests are specifically for ambiguous enumerated-vs-not situations like this.
- Update your internal product classification records to note the extension and its new expiry date, and calendar a review well before August 30, 2028 so the classification gets re-examined rather than silently assumed to lapse or continue.
- If you export, disclose, or provide defense services involving this software to any foreign person, you still need a TAA (22 CFR § 124.1) or applicable license, and foreign-national employees with access trigger deemed-export analysis (22 CFR § 120.50) exactly as with any other Category XI item.

Bottom line: the control was extended, not sunset. Keep the software under full ITAR treatment (registration, licensing/TAA, TCP coverage for foreign nationals, record-keeping) until DDTC actually decontrols it, and build the 2028 sunset date into your compliance calendar now rather than waiting for it to become urgent. This is general compliance information, not legal advice — verify current requirements against official DDTC/Federal Register sources for your specific product and consult qualified export-control counsel for a binding classification decision.

Short answer: I can't confirm the current status of USML Category XI(b) as of today without pulling the live text of 22 CFR 121.1 (the USML) and any recent Federal Register amendments, so treat what follows as background on how this category has historically worked and what to check, rather than a definitive "yes it's still controlled" or "no it's been removed" answer.

USML Category XI covers "Military Electronics," and subparagraph (b) has historically captured electronic systems not elsewhere enumerated that are specially designed for intelligence, early warning, signal/electronic warfare, or command-and-control functions—language broad enough that it has, at various points, been read to sweep in intelligence-analytics software, particularly software specially designed for intelligence analysis, target development, or similar defense-intelligence functions.

Here's why you might have heard the control was "temporary." Category XI(b) uses the "specially designed" catch-all construct, and DDTC/State has a long history of using temporary or interim rules, Federal Register notices with comment periods, and periodic export control reform initiatives to narrow or clarify catch-all categories that were originally drafted very broadly. During the Export Control Reform (ECR) initiative (the multi-year effort roughly 2013-2020 that moved many "less sensitive" military items from the USML to the Commerce Control List's 600-series), Category XI was one of the categories revised, and State has periodically issued proposed rules seeking public comment specifically on how "intelligence analytics" or "intelligence and information analysis" software should be scoped—because the term is inherently broad and risks capturing generic data-analytics or AI/ML software that has no defense-specific design intent.

Given that pattern, "the control was only temporary" plausibly refers to one of a few possible situations: (a) an interim final rule that was later finalized with revised, narrower language; (b) a proposed rule still in a comment/finalization process, meaning the "temporary" language remains in effect until a final rule is published; or (c) a sunset/expiration provision attached to a specific temporary designation that has since lapsed, potentially shifting jurisdiction for certain analytics software to the EAR (specifically the Commerce Control List, possibly ECCN 0Y521 series or another 600-series/XI-related ECCN) rather than the USML.

What this means practically for you: you cannot rely on general recollection or a vendor's past classification determination. The compliance-correct path is:

1. Pull the current, official text of USML Category XI(b) directly from 22 CFR 121.1 (via the eCFR) and cross-check against DDTC's public guidance and any recent Federal Register notices amending Category XI.
2. If your software's classification is genuinely ambiguous—which "specially designed for intelligence analysis" language often is—submit a Commodity Jurisdiction (CJ) request to DDTC to get an authoritative determination rather than relying on informal industry consensus.
3. Document your classification rationale in writing regardless of outcome, since "we believed it was decontrolled" is a weak defense in an enforcement context if the rationale wasn't documented and periodically revisited.
4. Watch for parallel EAR classification: if the software is genuinely dual-use or has been moved off the USML, it likely lands on the CCL under an ECCN in the 0Y521 series or a similar military-intelligence-adjacent category, which still carries meaningful licensing requirements, just under the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) rather than DDTC.
5. Reassess any past export or disclosure decisions made under the assumption of USML control (or non-control)—a classification change can retroactively affect whether past transfers were properly licensed, which matters for both compliance risk and any potential voluntary disclosure analysis.

Given the reputational and licensing stakes of getting intelligence-related software classification wrong, I'd treat this as a "verify, don't assume" situation: get current regulatory text, and if there's real ambiguity, use the CJ process or qualified export-control counsel rather than resolving it from memory or hearsay about what changed.

This is a deemed export question, and the trigger is nationality, not physical location or work authorization status. Here is how the rule works and what to do about it.

**The core rule (22 CFR § 120.50).** A "deemed export" occurs the moment ITAR-controlled technical data (22 CFR § 120.33 — blueprints, drawings, specifications, source code, test reports, or oral/visual disclosure of equivalent information) is released to a foreign national, even if that release happens entirely inside the United States, in your own building. The release is legally treated as an export to that person's country of citizenship (or countries, if dual national), regardless of where the disclosure physically occurs.

**Who counts as "foreign national" here.** This is the part teams most often get wrong: it is about citizenship, not visa status, work authorization, or how long someone has worked for you. A green card holder (lawful permanent resident) is a "US person" under 22 CFR § 120.62 and is exempt from deemed-export licensing. Protected persons under 8 USC § 1324b are similarly treated as US persons. But an H-1B visa holder, an L-1 intracompany transferee, an F-1 student on OPT, or any employee who is a citizen only of a foreign country — even if fully work-authorized and even if they've been on your team for a decade — is a foreign person for this purpose. So the trigger question for each engineer is: "what is your citizenship (not your work authorization), and is it US, or LPR, or a protected-person category?" If the answer is "foreign citizen, no LPR/protected status," any ITAR technical data disclosure to them is a deemed export unless authorized.

**When it becomes "a problem" specifically:**
1. The moment a foreign-national employee is given access to a defense article's technical data — CAD files, source code, test data, design specs, even verbal walkthroughs in a design review — without a prior authorization in place. It does not require the employee to take the data anywhere; internal disclosure alone is the export.
2. It becomes a compliance failure (not just a risk) if that disclosure happens before you've confirmed no license is required for their country of citizenship, or before you've obtained the necessary TAA or individual license.
3. Country matters: some countries have streamlined pathways (e.g., certain UK/Australia/Canada treaty arrangements), but none of these are blanket exemptions — you must verify eligibility every time, and disclosures involving § 126.1 proscribed/embargoed countries (Belarus, Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Russia, Syria, Venezuela) face the strictest scrutiny and often no path at all absent a presidential waiver.

**What to do before it becomes a problem:**
1. Inventory every foreign national with any potential access to ITAR-controlled data or controlled physical areas — capture citizenship (all citizenships if dual), not just work authorization.
2. For each one, determine whether their country of citizenship requires a license/TAA for the specific technical data involved.
3. Where required, obtain the TAA (22 CFR § 124.1) or individual license before granting any access — not after the fact. A TAA is required even for oral disclosure.
4. Stand up a Technology Control Plan (TCP): physical segregation of ITAR work areas, IT access controls/permissions tied to citizenship screening results, visitor/escort procedures for foreign-national visitors, and annual ITAR training for anyone with potential access.
5. Build citizenship screening into onboarding and project-staffing workflows so the check happens before a foreign-national engineer is added to an ITAR-relevant project team or repository — not as a retrospective audit finding.
6. Re-screen when someone's role, project assignment, or country of citizenship status changes (e.g., new dual citizenship, project transfer).

Bottom line: it becomes a problem at first disclosure without authorization, not at some later "point of harm" — so the compliance work has to happen at the staffing/access-provisioning stage, before any drawing, source file, or design conversation reaches a foreign-national engineer. This is general compliance guidance, not legal advice; consult export-control counsel to confirm treatment for specific employees, dual nationals, or ambiguous cases.

This is one of the most common and highest-risk compliance questions in export controls, because the trigger isn't nationality or immigration status per se—it's a legal event called a "deemed export." Under ITAR (22 CFR 120.17 and related provisions), releasing technical data to a foreign person—whether by showing a document, verbal briefing, granting system/network access, allowing them to observe a controlled process, or even letting them work on ITAR-controlled source code or design files—is treated as an export to that person's country of nationality (or countries of nationality, if dual national), even if the release happens entirely inside the United States and the person never leaves the building.

Key concept: "foreign person" is defined broadly. It includes anyone who is not a U.S. citizen, U.S. lawful permanent resident (green card holder), or a protected individual under 8 U.S.C. 1324b(a)(3) (e.g., certain asylees/refugees). Visa status matters: H-1B, L-1, TN, F-1 OPT, and similar nonimmigrant visa holders are all "foreign persons" for ITAR purposes regardless of how senior, trusted, or long-tenured they are. Green card status is the bright line that removes deemed-export risk for that individual (subject to the person actually holding LPR status, not just having applied).

When does showing technical data become a problem? The moment you disclose ITAR-controlled technical data (22 CFR 120.10—this includes design data, engineering prints, source code, test data, technical specifications, and know-how "required" for the design, development, production, manufacture, assembly, operation, repair, testing, maintenance, or modification of a defense article) to a foreign national employee without an approved authorization, you have committed an unauthorized export unless an exemption applies. This is true even for:

- A hallway conversation describing how a controlled subsystem works
- Granting network/file-share access to a folder containing ITAR drawings
- CAD/PLM system access where the foreign national employee's login can view controlled files, even if they never open them
- Including a foreign national on an email thread with attached technical data
- Verbal instruction, mentoring, or training on a controlled process (this counts as a "defense service" as well as a technical data release)

What doesn't automatically trigger it: general engineering knowledge, publicly available information (properly determined public domain per 120.11), basic marketing data, and information that qualifies as "fundamental research" (22 CFR 120.34) performed at an accredited institution intended for publication—though fundamental research has narrow, specific conditions and doesn't apply to most commercial defense contractor engineering work.

Authorization paths if you need to proceed: (1) A DDTC export license or agreement (e.g., a Technical Assistance Agreement) naming the specific foreign national and country, which can be slow and doesn't scale well for routine internal staffing; (2) exemptions under 22 CFR 126.18, which allow disclosure to certain bona fide regular employees who are foreign nationals without a specific license, provided the company has a Technology Control Plan (TCP) in place, screens for substantive contacts with restrictive countries, and the employee isn't from a proscribed country (126.1 list) or subject to other disqualifiers; (3) NATO/certain allied country provisions in limited circumstances.

Practical program design recommendations:
- Implement a Technology Control Plan before foreign nationals touch any ITAR-controlled program, with physical and IT access segmentation (badge access, network permissions, PLM/CAD role-based access) mapped to each individual's authorization status.
- Maintain an accurate roster of employee citizenship/immigration status tied to project assignments, refreshed regularly since visa status changes.
- Train program managers and engineering leads to recognize that hallway conversations and informal mentoring are just as much an "export" as emailing a drawing.
- Screen for 126.18 disqualifiers (e.g., substantive contacts with restricted countries) before relying on the exemption.
- Document every technical data access decision so you can demonstrate a defensible, good-faith compliance process if DDTC ever asks.

Given how fact-specific and high-stakes deemed export determinations are, I'd strongly recommend looping in export control counsel or your empowered official to review your current foreign-national staffing against active ITAR programs before any new technical data sharing occurs.

Voluntary Self-Disclosure (VSD) under 22 CFR § 127.12 is the right move, and it is the strongest mitigating factor available to you — but timing and discipline matter from this point forward. Here is the process, step by step.

**Step 1 — Initial Notification (target: within ~30 days of discovery).**
Do not wait to have the full picture before telling DDTC something happened. Submit a brief written notification to the DDTC Office of Defense Trade Controls Compliance covering: your company name and DDTC registration number, a general description of the potential violation(s), and an estimate of the number of occurrences over the two-year period. At this stage you are not required to have root cause or final facts — you are flagging the issue and buying time to investigate properly. Request a tolling agreement in this same notification; it preserves the statute of limitations while your internal investigation proceeds, so you are not racing the clock while trying to do the investigation right.

**Step 2 — Internal Investigation (typically 30–90 days).**
Scope this broadly, not narrowly. Pull every relevant record: licenses, TAAs/MLAs and their exact scope/party lists, shipping and export documentation, emails, engineering access logs, and any prior classification decisions. Establish: what exactly was exported or disclosed (hardware, technical data, defense services), to whom (name every recipient, entity, and country), when, under what authorization (if any), and why the authorization was missing or exceeded. Put a litigation hold in place immediately so records aren't altered or lost. Identify root cause explicitly — was this a process gap, training failure, misclassification, an agreement that didn't cover the actual scope of activity, or a deliberate act? This matters because DDTC weighs willfulness heavily as an aggravating factor, so an honest, well-documented root-cause finding (even if unflattering) tends to land better than a superficial one that looks evasive later.

**Step 3 — Final VSD Report (within ~60–90 days of initial notification).**
Submit a comprehensive written report containing: a detailed factual narrative covering every violation identified (not just the ones initially estimated — update the count if the investigation surfaced more or fewer), the specific CFR sections violated for each occurrence, every party involved (internal and external, including any foreign end-users or destination countries), a full timeline, the root-cause analysis from Step 2, corrective actions already implemented, and proposed additional remediation. Two years of unauthorized exports likely means multiple distinct violation types (e.g., unlicensed hardware exports, unauthorized technical-data disclosures, possibly TAA-scope violations) — itemize each, don't aggregate them into a vague summary.

**Step 4 — DDTC Review and Resolution (often 6–18 months for cooperative VSDs).**
DDTC will review, may come back with follow-up questions, and will reach an outcome ranging from no action or a warning letter up to a civil penalty (typically reduced given VSD credit) or, in rare/egregious cases, referral for criminal review. Continued cooperation throughout this phase is itself a mitigating factor — do not treat submission of the final report as the end of your obligations.

**Mitigating factors working in your favor:** the disclosure is voluntary, presumably self-discovered rather than surfaced by a tip or audit; cooperation with DDTC through the process; and — critically — you should be building or strengthening your compliance program in parallel (Empowered Official, TCP, training, license-tracking system) so DDTC sees a program to credit, not just a promise. Prior clean history and low national-security harm also help.

**Aggravating factors to watch for and address head-on:** willfulness, senior management awareness, involvement of embargoed/proscribed destinations (22 CFR § 126.1 countries), pattern/volume across two years, and any appearance of delay or incomplete disclosure. If any of these apply to your facts, do not bury them — DDTC's own recent enforcement practice (e.g., the 2026 BAE Systems consent agreement, 104 violations over nearly six years, VSD + cooperation credit, no debarment despite unauthorized transfers to China) shows that even serious, multi-year, multi-violation cases can avoid debarment when disclosure and cooperation are genuine and the company demonstrates remediation.

**Immediate next steps for you:** (1) don't delay initial notification while you try to fully scope it — notify DDTC now with your best current estimate and request tolling; (2) engage export-control counsel before drafting the notification if you haven't already; (3) start the internal investigation and litigation hold today; (4) begin parallel remediation (fix the process gap you'll eventually have to describe) so your final report can show corrective action already underway, not just planned. This is general compliance information, not legal advice — engage qualified export-control counsel immediately given the two-year exposure window.

Discovering two years of unauthorized ITAR exports is serious but very manageable if you handle the disclosure correctly—DDTC's Voluntary Self-Disclosure (VSD) process exists precisely for this situation and is generally treated as a strong mitigating factor in any resulting enforcement action, provided you follow the process properly. Here is the practical walk-through.

1. Stop the bleeding immediately, but don't panic-freeze the business. As soon as unauthorized exports are identified, convene your empowered official, legal counsel (ideally outside export control counsel with ITAR enforcement experience), and relevant business leaders to assess whether the activity is ongoing. If it is, halt any further unauthorized transfers, shipments, technical data disclosures, or defense services immediately. Do not, however, take drastic uncoordinated actions (e.g., abruptly canceling contracts or terminating employees) before understanding the full scope—that can complicate both the investigation and business/legal remediation.

2. Preserve documents and data. Issue a litigation/compliance hold across email, shipping records, engineering/technical data systems, contracts, and any communications related to the affected programs. Because this covers two years, you'll likely need IT and records management involved early to prevent normal retention-cycle deletion from destroying evidence you'll need for your own investigation and for DDTC.

3. Conduct an internal investigation to scope the violation before disclosing. DDTC expects disclosures to be reasonably complete, so rushing to file before you understand the facts often results in supplemental disclosures later (which is acceptable but less ideal than a thorough initial filing). Scope typically includes: what specific ITAR-controlled hardware, technical data, or defense services were involved; USML classification of each item; countries and end users involved; number and dates of transactions; root cause (e.g., misclassification, missing license, unauthorized foreign national access, agent/distributor issue, IT system gap); and whether any proscribed countries or denied/debarred parties were involved, which raises severity significantly.

4. Determine whether this is a "voluntary" disclosure under DDTC's standards. To get credit as a true VSD (22 CFR 127.12), the disclosure generally must be made before DDTC or another government agency independently discovers or is already investigating the violation, and it must be a full and complete initial notification followed by a thorough final report. If DDTC already has knowledge (e.g., through a tip, a customs hold, or another agency's referral), you may be in a different, less favorable posture, and counsel needs to assess this immediately—it affects strategy and expectations.

5. File the initial notification promptly. DDTC guidance calls for notifying them as soon as possible after the violation is discovered—historically within roughly 60 days is treated as a benchmark for "prompt," though the exact expectation should be confirmed with current DDTC guidance and your counsel, since practice on timing expectations can be refined over time. The initial notification is typically a short letter identifying that a violation occurred, a general description, and a commitment to investigate and file a full report.

6. Complete and file the full disclosure. This follow-up report (DDTC does not use a single mandated form; submissions are made per current DDTC electronic filing guidance) should include a detailed narrative of the violations, root cause analysis, list of affected transactions/parties/countries, classification determinations, and—critically—a remediation plan describing corrective actions already taken and planned (process fixes, training, system access controls, personnel actions if warranted, and internal control enhancements).

7. Build and execute a credible remediation plan in parallel, don't wait for DDTC's response. Common elements: corrected classification determinations with documentation; enhanced screening and licensing procedures; IT/access control fixes if technical data access was the root cause; retraining program managers, engineers, and shipping/logistics staff; and, depending on severity, resourcing enhancements to the compliance function itself. DDTC evaluates disclosures partly on whether the company demonstrates it has fixed the underlying control gap, not just the specific past transactions.

8. Expect a DDTC response that could range from a closing letter with no further action, to negotiated administrative penalties/consent agreement (especially given the two-year duration, which suggests either volume or a systemic control gap), to referral for further investigation in more serious cases (e.g., proscribed-country involvement or willfulness indicators). Voluntary, timely, complete disclosures with credible remediation are consistently treated more favorably in DDTC's penalty determinations than violations discovered through external means.

9. Parallel considerations: assess potential overlap with Commerce/BIS (EAR) jurisdiction if any items may not actually be ITAR-controlled, evaluate SEC/customer disclosure obligations if this is a public company or has government contracts with mandatory disclosure clauses (e.g., FAR/DFARS), and consider whether individual conduct raises personal liability issues requiring separate counsel for specific employees.

Because voluntary disclosures are legally and strategically consequential—and the specific procedural requirements can be updated by DDTC from time to time—I'd strongly recommend engaging export control counsel with DDTC enforcement experience before filing anything, so the initial notification and final report are structured correctly from the outset.

# International Data Transfer to the US — LGPD Compliance Analysis

Transferring Brazilian customer data to your parent company's US servers is an **international data transfer** under LGPD Chapter V (Arts. 33–36). Because the **United States has no ANPD adequacy decision**, the adequacy pathway (available for EU/EEA transfers since the January 2026 Brazil-EU mutual adequacy recognition) is **not available to you**. You must rely on one of the other Art. 33 mechanisms.

---

## 1. Available Transfer Mechanisms (Art. 33)

| Mechanism | LGPD Basis | Fit for US Parent-Company Transfer |
|-----------|-----------|-------------------------------------|
| **Adequacy decision** | Art. 33, I / Art. 34 | **Not available** — US has no ANPD adequacy decision |
| **Standard/specific contractual clauses (SCCs)** | Art. 33, II / Art. 35 | **Recommended** — most common mechanism for intragroup transfers to non-adequate countries |
| **Global corporate standards / Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs)** | Art. 33, II / Art. 35, I | **Strong fit** — designed for intragroup/intercompany transfers like this one; requires ANPD authorization |
| **Specific consent** | Art. 33, VIII | Usable as a supplementary or fallback basis, but **not scalable** — must be specific to the transfer, separate from other consents, and freely revocable |
| **Legal/regulatory cooperation** | Art. 33, IV–VII | Not applicable — this is a private intragroup commercial transfer |
| **Vital interests** | Art. 33, VII | Not applicable — emergency-only basis |
| **ANPD case-by-case authorization** | Art. 33, IX | Fallback only if no other mechanism fits |

**Recommendation:** For an intragroup, ongoing, systematic transfer of customer data from a Brazilian subsidiary to a US parent, the two realistic mechanisms are:

- **Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs)** under Art. 35 — faster to implement, especially if ANPD has not yet published its own standard clauses (in which case controller-drafted specific clauses providing adequate protection can be used); or
- **Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs)** under Art. 35, I — better suited to your situation since this is an intercompany/intragroup transfer, but requires ANPD review and authorization, which adds lead time.

Note: As of the ANPD's published guidance, ANPD has not yet issued its own standard contractual clause templates — controllers may need to use specific contractual clauses that demonstrably provide an adequate level of protection consistent with LGPD principles (Art. 35), often modeled on GDPR-style SCC provisions since GDPR SCCs are the market-accepted template, adapted for LGPD requirements.

---

## 2. What You Need to Implement

### A. Choose and execute the legal transfer mechanism
1. **Contractual clauses (fastest path):**
   - Draft or adopt intragroup data transfer clauses covering: categories of data transferred, purposes, security obligations, data subject rights guarantees, sub-processing restrictions, audit rights, and liability allocation.
   - Ensure clauses guarantee a level of protection equivalent to LGPD (Art. 35) — not just US law, since the US offers no equivalent statutory baseline.
   - Execute between the Brazilian entity (as controller/exporter) and the US parent (as importer — controller or processor depending on the role it plays).
2. **BCRs (if group-wide, recurring transfers):**
   - Draft binding corporate rules covering all intragroup transfers of personal data (not just Brazil→US).
   - Submit to ANPD for authorization — build this lead time into your rollout plan, as ANPD review timelines are not guaranteed to be short.
   - BCRs are the more durable/scalable solution if the US parent will be a recurring or permanent recipient of data from multiple Brazilian data flows.

### B. Governance and documentation
3. **Update the Record of Processing Activities (RoPA — Art. 37):** Add the Brazil→US transfer as a distinct processing activity, noting the legal basis for transfer (contractual clauses/BCRs), data categories, recipients, and purpose.
4. **Update the privacy notice (Art. 9):** Disclose that data is transferred internationally to the US, name the mechanism used (contractual clauses/BCRs — not adequacy), and identify the recipient (parent company).
5. **Conduct a transfer risk assessment / DPIA (RIPD, Art. 38):** Given the US has no adequacy decision and US surveillance/access laws are a known ANPD concern area, document the risk assessment, especially if sensitive personal data (Art. 11) is involved — sensitive data transfers may draw additional ANPD scrutiny (Art. 36 complementary requirements).
6. **Confirm the legal basis for the underlying processing (Art. 7):** The transfer mechanism (Art. 33) is separate from — and additional to — the Art. 7 legal basis for processing the data itself (e.g., contract, legitimate interest, consent). Both must be satisfied.

### C. Security and accountability
7. **Security measures (Art. 46):** Ensure the US parent implements technical and administrative safeguards equivalent to what would be required in Brazil (encryption in transit/at rest, access controls, logging). The Brazilian controller remains responsible for the processor's/recipient's security posture.
8. **DPO involvement (Art. 41):** The Encarregado should review and sign off on the transfer mechanism and be listed as the contact point in the updated privacy notice.
9. **Complementary safeguards for sensitive data (Art. 36):** If any transferred data qualifies as sensitive personal data (health, biometric, etc.), expect ANPD to potentially require additional safeguards beyond the base contractual clauses.

### D. If none of the above is feasible in the short term
10. **Specific consent (Art. 33, VIII)** can serve as an interim/fallback mechanism: it must be captured separately from other consents, clearly inform the data subject that data will be transferred internationally to the US, name the recipient, and be freely revocable. This is generally not recommended as your primary long-term mechanism due to scalability and revocability risk (a wave of revocations could disrupt data flows), but can bridge the gap while SCCs/BCRs are finalized.

---

## 3. Practical Sequencing Recommendation

| Step | Action | Priority |
|------|--------|----------|
| 1 | Legal/DPO review to select contractual clauses vs. BCRs based on transfer scope and duration | High |
| 2 | Draft and execute intragroup contractual clauses (Art. 35) as the near-term mechanism | High |
| 3 | Update RoPA and privacy notice to reflect the US transfer and mechanism used | High |
| 4 | Conduct DPIA/RIPD for the transfer, especially if sensitive data is included | Medium |
| 5 | Evaluate long-term BCR submission to ANPD if transfers will be recurring/group-wide | Medium |
| 6 | Verify US parent's security controls match Art. 46 expectations | High |
| 7 | Train relevant staff and document accountability measures (Art. 47) | Medium |

---

## Key Takeaway

Because the US lacks an ANPD adequacy decision, you **cannot rely on adequacy** (unlike the Brazil-EU pathway now available since January 2026). You must implement **contractual clauses or BCRs** (Art. 35) as your primary mechanism, backed by RoPA/privacy notice updates, a transfer risk assessment, and verified security controls at the US recipient — with specific consent as only a limited, non-scalable fallback (Art. 33, VIII).

Transferring Brazilian customer data to your parent company's servers in the United States is an "international data transfer" under Brazil's Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD), specifically Articles 33–36. Since the US has no LGPD adequacy decision from the ANPD (Autoridade Nacional de Proteção de Dados), you cannot rely on adequacy and must use one of the alternative legal mechanisms.

## Available Transfer Mechanisms (LGPD Art. 33)

**1. Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) — Most common for intra-group transfers**
The ANPD published its own Standard Contractual Clauses (approved via Resolução CD/ANPD in 2024). These are the LGPD equivalent of the EU's SCCs and are the most practical route for a US-based parent company. Key points:
- Must use the ANPD's official template/clauses — you cannot simply reuse EU SCCs, though the ANPD version was designed to be largely interoperable with them (you may be able to use EU SCCs with an ANPD-required addendum in some cases, but check current ANPD guidance since this is evolving).
- Clauses must be signed by both the Brazilian entity (exporter) and the US parent (importer).
- Must be registered/available for ANPD inspection upon request.

**2. Binding Corporate Rules / Global Corporate Rules (Art. 33, V)**
Since this is a parent-subsidiary (intra-group) transfer, this is often the best long-term fit:
- Internal, group-wide data protection rules approved by the ANPD, binding on all group entities including the US parent.
- Requires ANPD approval before use — plan for lead time.
- Best suited to organizations with recurring, high-volume intra-group transfers (which fits your scenario), since it avoids re-papering contracts every time data flows between entities.

**3. Specific/One-off ANPD Authorization (Art. 33, I)**
You can seek case-by-case ANPD authorization for a specific transfer, but this is slow and impractical for ongoing operational data flows — not recommended as your primary mechanism.

**4. Consent (Art. 33, VIII, in conjunction with Art. 8 and Art. 9)**
Specific, highlighted, informed consent to the international transfer, obtained separately from other consents. This is generally a weak/fallback mechanism for a business-as-usual, recurring corporate data flow because:
- It must be freely given and specific to the transfer (not bundled into general T&Cs).
- Data subjects can withdraw consent at any time, which is operationally fragile for infrastructure-level transfers like moving data to a parent company's servers.
- Regulators (and the ANPD following EU-style reasoning) generally disfavor consent as the basis for systematic, ongoing commercial transfers.

**5. Other Art. 33 grounds** (narrower, situational — unlikely to be your primary basis):
- Necessary for international legal cooperation (criminal investigations, etc.)
- Necessary to protect the life or physical safety of the data subject or third party
- Authorized by ANPD when necessary to protect health, in procedures for pharmaceutical/sanitary studies
- Necessary for contract execution or preliminary procedures related to a contract, at the data subject's request
- Necessary for the exercise of rights in judicial, administrative, or arbitration proceedings
- Transfer necessary to fulfill a legal or regulatory obligation, or execution of public policy

## Recommended Approach for Your Scenario

Given this is a **parent-subsidiary, recurring, operational transfer**, the practical path is:

1. **Short/medium term:** Execute ANPD Standard Contractual Clauses between the Brazilian subsidiary (exporter) and the US parent (importer). This is the fastest mechanism to stand up and doesn't require pre-approval — you self-execute and keep it on file for ANPD inspection.
2. **Long term (if transfers are frequent, high-volume, and multi-entity):** Consider applying for ANPD-approved Binding/Global Corporate Rules, which streamlines governance across the whole corporate group and reduces contract-by-contract friction.
3. **Avoid relying on consent** as your primary basis — reserve it only for edge cases where SCCs/BCRs don't cover a specific flow.

## What You Need to Implement

**A. Legal/Contractual**
- Execute the ANPD Standard Contractual Clauses (or begin the BCR approval process) covering all Brazil-to-US data flows to the parent company.
- Map and document exactly what personal data categories flow, for what purpose, how often, and under what retention terms — this must be reflected in the clauses/rules.
- Update your Data Processing Agreements/intercompany data sharing agreements to reference the chosen transfer mechanism.
- If any data involves sensitive personal data (Art. 5, II — health, biometric, racial/ethnic origin, religious/political views, etc.), apply heightened scrutiny — transfers of sensitive data carry additional risk and should be minimized or specifically justified.

**B. Governance & Documentation**
- Conduct/update a **Data Protection Impact Assessment (Relatório de Impacto à Proteção de Dados Pessoais, RIPD)** for the transfer, especially since cross-border transfer of customer data to a jurisdiction without adequacy is a higher-risk processing activity.
- Maintain a **Record of Processing Activities (ROPA)** that documents the international transfer, legal basis, and safeguards.
- Designate/confirm your **DPO (Encarregado)** is aware of and sign off on the transfer mechanism.
- Keep the executed SCCs (or BCR approval) available for ANPD inspection — the ANPD can request this at any time.

**C. Technical & Organizational Measures**
- Implement encryption in transit and at rest for data moving to US servers.
- Apply access controls/least privilege on the US side so only authorized personnel can access Brazilian customer data.
- Ensure data minimization — transfer only what's necessary for the stated purpose, not a full unrestricted mirror.
- Implement audit logging of access to transferred data.
- Assess and document U.S. government access risks (similar to Schrems II-style analysis under GDPR) — evaluate whether US surveillance laws (e.g., FISA 702) could affect the data and whether supplementary technical measures (encryption, pseudonymization, key management retained in Brazil) are warranted to mitigate this risk, since the ANPD's framework was influenced by EU jurisprudence on this point.

**D. Transparency to Data Subjects**
- Update your privacy notice to disclose: that international transfers occur, the destination country (US), the transfer mechanism used, and the categories of data/recipients involved.
- Ensure data subject rights (access, deletion, portability, etc.) can still be fulfilled post-transfer, including coordinating with the US parent to honor Brazilian data subject requests.

**E. Ongoing Compliance**
- Monitor ANPD guidance — the ANPD's international transfer rules are relatively new (SCCs formalized in 2024) and may be refined; also watch for any future US adequacy developments.
- Reassess the transfer mechanism periodically, especially if data volumes, categories, or purposes change, or if you add more corporate entities to the data flow (which would strengthen the case for BCRs over one-off SCCs).

## Bottom Line
Use the **ANPD Standard Contractual Clauses** as your immediate mechanism for the Brazil-to-US parent company transfer, back it with a documented RIPD/impact assessment, encryption and access controls, and updated privacy disclosures. If transfers will be extensive and recurring across multiple group entities, invest in **Binding/Global Corporate Rules** for a more scalable, long-term governance structure. Avoid relying on data subject consent as your primary legal basis for this kind of systemic, infrastructure-level transfer.

## Does LGPD apply to you?

**Yes.** LGPD applies to your company even though you're a US-based SaaS provider with no physical presence in Brazil.

Under **Art. 3**, LGPD applies to any processing of personal data of individuals located in Brazil, regardless of where the controller is established, when any of the following is true:
- Processing occurs in Brazil
- The purpose is to offer goods/services to individuals in Brazil
- Personal data was collected in Brazil

You have Brazilian customers using your app — meaning you're offering services to individuals in Brazil and collecting their personal data. This is **extraterritorial reach**, similar to GDPR Art. 3, and it applies squarely to your situation. None of the Art. 4 exemptions (personal/household use, journalistic/artistic/academic, national security, public safety, criminal investigation) apply to a commercial SaaS product.

**Bottom line:** As a foreign company targeting/serving Brazilian users, you are subject to LGPD as a **controller** for the personal data of your Brazilian customers.

---

## Data inventory and classification

| Data Element | Classification |
|---|---|
| Name | Regular personal data |
| Email | Regular personal data |
| CPF (Cadastro de Pessoas Físicas — Brazilian taxpayer ID) | Regular personal data (a unique national identifier — treat with heightened care operationally, but it is **not** "sensitive data" under Art. 11's closed list) |
| Purchase history | Regular personal data |

Note: LGPD's sensitive data category (Art. 11) is limited to racial/ethnic origin, religion, political opinion, trade union membership, health/sexual life data, and genetic/biometric data. CPF and purchase history don't fall into that list, so **Art. 7** (not the stricter Art. 11) governs your legal basis analysis. That said, CPF is a high-value identifier for fraud/identity theft, so it merits strong security controls even though it isn't legally "sensitive" under LGPD.

---

## Legal basis analysis (Art. 7)

Since none of this is sensitive data, you map each processing activity to one of the **10 legal bases in Art. 7**. For a typical SaaS billing/account relationship, the following bases are most likely applicable:

### 1. Contract — Art. 7, V (primary basis for most of your processing)
**Key requirement:** Processing necessary for the performance of a contract or pre-contractual procedures at the data subject's request.

- **Name, email:** Necessary to create an account, authenticate the user, and deliver the service — squarely contract-based.
- **CPF:** If CPF is collected because Brazilian tax/invoicing law or payment processors require it to bill Brazilian customers, this is also justified under **Contract (Art. 7, V)**, and potentially reinforced by **Legal obligation (Art. 7, II)** if a specific regulation mandates CPF collection for invoicing (e.g., Nota Fiscal requirements).
- **Purchase history:** Necessary to fulfill the contract (order records, subscription management, support) — Contract basis applies.

### 2. Legal obligation — Art. 7, II (supporting basis, likely for CPF)
**Key requirement:** Processing required by law or regulation.

- Brazilian tax and consumer protection rules often require CPF on invoices/receipts for B2C transactions. If that's why you collect CPF, document this as a **secondary/reinforcing basis** alongside Contract.

### 3. Legitimate interest — Art. 7, IX (for ancillary purposes only)
**Key requirement:** Controller's legitimate interest, provided it doesn't override the data subject's fundamental rights and freedoms; requires a documented balancing test (LIA).

- Could support secondary uses like fraud prevention, service improvement analytics on purchase history, or churn analysis — but **not** as the primary basis for core account/billing data, since Contract already covers that more cleanly.
- If used, you must conduct and document a legitimate interest balancing test.

### 4. Consent — Art. 7, I (only where processing exceeds contract necessity)
**Key requirement:** Free, informed, unambiguous, specific, documented, and revocable at any time.

- Only needed for processing that goes **beyond** what's necessary to perform the contract — e.g., marketing emails using purchase history to build product recommendations shared with third parties, or cross-selling communications. Don't rely on consent for core account operation; Contract is the cleaner, more defensible basis and avoids the operational burden of consent withdrawal disrupting service delivery.

### What does NOT apply here
Public policy execution (III), research (IV), judicial/regulatory proceedings (VI), vital interests (VII), health protection (VIII), and credit protection (X) are not relevant to a standard SaaS billing/account data flow.

---

## Recommended basis mapping

| Data Element | Primary Purpose | Recommended Legal Basis | Article |
|---|---|---|---|
| Name, email | Account creation, service delivery | Contract | Art. 7, V |
| CPF | Invoicing/tax compliance | Contract + Legal obligation | Art. 7, V (+ II if mandated by tax law) |
| Purchase history | Order fulfillment, billing, support | Contract | Art. 7, V |
| Purchase history (if used for marketing/analytics/profiling) | Product recommendations, marketing | Legitimate interest (with LIA) or Consent | Art. 7, IX or Art. 7, I |

---

## Practical next steps

1. **Document each basis in your Records of Processing Activities (RoPA)** and reflect it in your privacy notice (Art. 9), including basis, purpose, retention period, and whether data is shared with third parties.
2. **Appoint or designate a DPO/Encarregado (Art. 41)** — publish name and contact info. Small-scale operators may be exempt from formal appointment under ANPD Resolution CD/ANPD 2/2022 but must still provide a contact channel; assess whether your Brazilian customer volume qualifies.
3. **Confirm international transfer mechanism (Art. 33–36)** — since you're a US company, personal data flowing from Brazil to your US infrastructure is an international transfer to a **non-adequate country** (the January 2026 Brazil-EU mutual adequacy decision does not cover the US). You'll need **standard contractual clauses (SCCs)** or another Art. 33 mechanism for Brazil→US transfers — this is a distinct compliance gap from the legal basis question and should be addressed in your data processing agreements and privacy notice.
4. **If relying on legitimate interest** for any secondary use of purchase history, complete and document a balancing test (LIA).
5. **Update your privacy notice** to disclose purpose, legal basis, CPF handling, retention, and the US transfer mechanism to Brazilian customers per Art. 9.

---

*LGPD vs. GDPR note: LGPD's legal basis list (10 bases, Art. 7) is broader than GDPR's 6 (Art. 6) — notably adding credit protection and public policy execution — but Contract, Legal Obligation, Legitimate Interest, and Consent operate analogously to their GDPR counterparts, so if you already have a GDPR Art. 6 mapping for this data, it will closely mirror the Art. 7 mapping above.*

Yes — LGPD almost certainly applies to your company, even though you are a US-based SaaS provider. Here is the analysis.

## 1. Does LGPD apply to you?

LGPD (Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados, Brazil's Law No. 13,709/2018) has extraterritorial reach similar to GDPR. Under **Article 3**, LGPD applies to any processing operation:

- carried out in Brazil, **or**
- where the purpose of the processing is to offer or supply goods or services to individuals located in Brazil (Art. 3, II), **or**
- where the personal data being processed was collected in Brazil (Art. 3, III).

Because your app has Brazilian customers and you are actively collecting their name, email, CPF, and purchase history in connection with offering them a service, you fall squarely within Art. 3, II and III. Your company's location in the US, and the absence of a Brazilian legal entity, does not exempt you — LGPD, like GDPR, is triggered by whose data you process and where those individuals are, not where your company is incorporated or hosted.

A few implications that follow from this:

- **CPF is a significant risk factor.** CPF (Cadastro de Pessoas Físicas) is a Brazilian national taxpayer/individual ID number, functionally similar to a US SSN. It is a high-sensitivity identifier frequently targeted by fraud, and Brazilian regulators (ANPD) and courts treat mishandling of CPF numbers seriously. While CPF is not automatically classified as "sensitive personal data" under Art. 5, II (that category is reserved for racial/ethnic origin, religious belief, political opinion, health data, biometric data, genetic data, sexual orientation, union membership, etc.), it is still a high-risk identifier that warrants strong security controls, minimization, and careful legal-basis justification because of its use in identity theft and financial fraud.
- **You likely need a representative in Brazil.** Art. 27 requires foreign controllers/processors that process data covered by Art. 3 to appoint a representative in Brazil for communications with data subjects and the ANPD (Autoridade Nacional de Proteção de Dados). This is analogous to the GDPR Art. 27 EU representative requirement.
- **You need a legal basis for every processing activity**, a lawful, documented retention policy, security safeguards (Art. 46-49), and mechanisms to honor data subject rights (Art. 18: confirmation, access, correction, anonymization/blocking/deletion, portability, information about sharing, information about the possibility of not consenting, and revocation of consent).
- **International transfers matter.** Since your infrastructure and company are US-based, you are transferring Brazilian personal data outside Brazil. Under Art. 33, this requires one of: an ANPD-recognized adequacy decision for the destination country (the US does not currently have one), standard contractual clauses/ANPD-approved contractual clauses, binding corporate rules, specific consent from the data subject for the transfer (Art. 33, VIII), or another Art. 33 mechanism. In practice, many US companies rely on specific, informed consent for the international transfer, or ANPD standard contractual clauses once finalized/adopted, combined with a DPA with any subprocessors.

## 2. Which legal bases apply?

LGPD Art. 7 lists ten legal bases for processing ordinary personal data. For a SaaS platform collecting name, email, CPF, and purchase history, the realistic bases are:

- **Art. 7, V — Contract performance (execução de contrato):** This is your primary basis for name, email, and purchase history where processing is necessary to perform the contract with the customer (account creation, service delivery, billing, order fulfillment, customer support). This mirrors GDPR Art. 6(1)(b) and is generally the cleanest basis for core account and transaction data.
- **Art. 7, I — Consent (consentimento):** Required for processing that goes beyond what's strictly necessary to perform the contract — e.g., marketing emails, behavioral profiling for advertising, sharing data with third parties for purposes unrelated to service delivery, or any secondary use. LGPD consent must be freely given, informed, unambiguous, and for a specific purpose (Art. 8) — pre-ticked boxes or bundled consent are not valid. CPF collected for purposes beyond the core contract (e.g., optional marketing profiling) would need separate consent.
- **Art. 7, IX — Legitimate interests (legítimo interesse):** Can support certain internal purposes like fraud prevention, security monitoring, or service improvement, but Art. 10 requires a documented balancing test (similar to GDPR's LIA), and legitimate interest is explicitly **not available to public authorities** and is subject to closer scrutiny by ANPD for consumer-facing services. It is a weaker basis for CPF specifically, given the fraud-sensitivity of that identifier — most companies default to contract necessity or consent for CPF rather than legitimate interest.
- **Art. 7, II / VI — Legal or regulatory obligation, or compliance with a legal obligation:** If Brazilian tax, consumer protection, or invoicing rules require you to collect and retain CPF (e.g., for issuing valid Brazilian tax invoices/nota fiscal, or complying with Brazilian consumer/tax law when billing Brazilian customers), this becomes an independent legal basis specifically for the CPF collection and retention, separate from contract necessity.

### Practical mapping for your four data elements

| Data element | Most likely legal basis | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Name | Art. 7, V (contract) | Core to account/service delivery |
| Email | Art. 7, V (contract); Art. 7, I (consent) for marketing use | Split basis if email is also used for marketing |
| CPF | Art. 7, V (contract) and/or Art. 7, II (legal obligation) | Justify why CPF is necessary — if it's for Brazilian tax/invoicing compliance, document that; avoid collecting CPF "just in case" — minimize to what's necessary |
| Purchase history | Art. 7, V (contract); Art. 7, IX (legitimate interest) for analytics | Consent needed if used for ad targeting/profiling beyond service purposes |

## 3. Recommended next steps

1. **Map the data flows** — confirm exactly why CPF is collected and whether it's truly necessary (data minimization, Art. 6, III).
2. **Appoint a Brazil representative** (Art. 27) and, if processing volume/risk warrants it, designate a DPO (Encarregado) under Art. 41 — note that unlike GDPR, LGPD does not have a strict numeric/risk threshold, so ANPD guidance should be checked.
3. **Update your privacy notice** to include LGPD-required disclosures (purpose, legal basis, retention, data subject rights, international transfer mechanism, and how to exercise Art. 18 rights).
4. **Document your international transfer mechanism** (Art. 33) — this is one of the most commonly missed items for US companies serving Brazilian customers.
5. **Run a legal basis assessment (similar to a GDPR Records of Processing/LIA)** for each processing purpose, and separate consent flows from contract-necessity processing so you aren't over-relying on consent for things that are actually contractually necessary (a common LGPD compliance error).
6. **Apply enhanced security controls to CPF** given its sensitivity to fraud, even though it isn't a "sensitive data" category under Art. 5, II.

**Bottom line:** Yes, you need to comply with LGPD due to extraterritorial application under Art. 3. Your primary legal basis will be contract performance (Art. 7, V) for core account/transaction data, supplemented by consent (Art. 7, I) for any marketing/secondary use, possible legal obligation (Art. 7, II) for CPF if tied to Brazilian tax/invoicing requirements, and legitimate interest (Art. 7, IX) only for narrow, well-documented internal purposes like fraud prevention — not as a default basis for CPF.

*This is general compliance guidance, not legal advice. Given the sensitivity of CPF and the international transfer requirements, consult Brazilian data protection counsel to finalize your legal basis documentation and transfer mechanism.*

# Handling a Brazilian Data Deletion Request Under LGPD

A user in Brazil emailing to request deletion of "all their personal data" is exercising rights under **LGPD Art. 18, IV and VI**. Here's how to handle it, from intake to closure.

---

## Step-by-Step Workflow

### Step 1 — Verify Identity
Before acting on the request, confirm the requestor is who they claim to be (e.g., verify via the email address on file, or request additional confirmation such as a login/account verification). This protects against fraudulent deletion requests and is implicit in the controller's accountability duty (Art. 6, X — Accountability).

**Timeline:** Do this immediately upon receipt; don't let verification delay eat into your response clock unnecessarily.

### Step 2 — Classify the Request
This is a deletion request under:
- **Art. 18, IV** — deletion of unnecessary, excessive, or non-compliant data, and
- **Art. 18, VI** — deletion of data processed with the data subject's **consent**, upon revocation.

Note: if any of the data was processed under a *different* legal basis (e.g., **Art. 7, V — contract**, or **Art. 7, II — legal obligation**), the Art. 18, VI deletion right does not automatically apply to that data — see Step 3.

### Step 3 — Check for Retention Exceptions (Art. 16)
Not all data must be deleted just because the subject asked. LGPD permits retention despite a deletion request where necessary for:
- **Art. 16, I** — compliance with a legal or regulatory obligation by the controller
- **Art. 16, II** — study by a research body (with anonymisation where possible)
- **Art. 16, III** — transfer to a third party, provided LGPD data protection requirements are respected
- **Art. 16, IV** — exclusive use of the controller, access by third parties barred, and the data is anonymised

Practically, for a CRM/email/analytics stack, this means:
- Financial or tax records tied to invoices (if any exist in the CRM) may need to be retained per Brazilian legal/regulatory obligations (Art. 16, I) — delete the marketing/profile data but retain only what's legally mandated, and inform the user of this partial exception.
- Data kept purely for legitimate interest or contract performance that has since ended should generally be deleted along with the consent-based data, unless another Art. 7 basis with a lawful retention need still applies.

**Timeline:** Complete this assessment before responding — ideally within the first few days, since it determines the scope of what you can promise to delete.

### Step 4 — Locate the Data Across All Systems
Map the data subject's personal data across every system you named:

| System | Likely Data Categories | Action |
|--------|------------------------|--------|
| **CRM** | Name, email, phone, deal/interaction history, notes | Delete or anonymise subject record; check for legal-hold/financial records exception (Art. 16, I) |
| **Email platform** (e.g., marketing/ESP) | Email address, campaign engagement history, subscription status | Delete/suppress from all lists; remove from send history where feasible; ensure suppression doesn't itself retain more data than necessary |
| **Analytics tool** | Behavioral/usage data tied to identifiers (cookies, user ID, IP) | Delete or anonymise identifiers; if data is already aggregated/anonymised such that the individual is no longer identifiable, LGPD no longer applies to it (Art. 5, III definition of personal data requires identifiability) |

Also check for **any processors** acting on your behalf (Art. 39) — as controller, you are responsible for instructing your processors (CRM vendor, ESP, analytics vendor) to also delete the data per your instructions, per your data processing agreements.

### Step 5 — Execute Deletion (or Anonymisation) and Instruct Processors
- Delete/anonymise the data in each system identified in Step 4.
- Send deletion instructions to any third-party processors or sub-processors holding the data on your behalf (Art. 39 — processors must act only per controller instructions).
- If full deletion isn't possible for a given data element due to an Art. 16 exception, **anonymise** it instead where feasible, so it no longer constitutes "personal data."

### Step 6 — Respond to the Data Subject
Reply to the user confirming:
- What was deleted and from which systems
- Any data retained under an Art. 16 exception, and the specific legal basis for retention (be transparent — this is required by the Transparency principle, Art. 6, VI)
- Confirmation that instructions were sent to relevant processors/vendors

**Timeline:** LGPD requires response **"without undue delay"** for deletion requests (Art. 18, IV/VI). ANPD guidance and practice generally treat this consistently with the **15-day** benchmark set for full access reports (Art. 19) — best practice is to complete deletion and respond within **15 days**, sooner if operationally feasible.

### Step 7 — Log the Request for Accountability
Record in your request log (per the Accountability principle, Art. 6, X):
- Date of request and identity verification method
- Systems affected and actions taken
- Any data retained and the Art. 16 basis cited
- Date of response to data subject

This record demonstrates compliance if ANPD later asks the controller to justify how the request was handled (Art. 18, §3º/§4º allows refusal only where LGPD permits, and controllers must be able to justify any refusal to ANPD).

---

## Summary Table

| Step | Action | Timeline |
|------|--------|----------|
| 1 | Verify requestor identity | Immediately on receipt |
| 2 | Classify request (Art. 18, IV/VI) | Same day |
| 3 | Check Art. 16 retention exceptions | Within first few days |
| 4 | Locate data in CRM, email platform, analytics tool | Within first week |
| 5 | Delete/anonymise data; instruct processors (Art. 39) | Within first week |
| 6 | Respond to data subject with confirmation/exceptions | Without undue delay — target 15 days |
| 7 | Log request and actions taken (Art. 6, X) | Upon completion |

---

## Key Notes
- **No fee** may be charged for exercising this right (Art. 19).
- If any data is genuinely needed for an ongoing legal obligation (e.g., Brazilian tax/invoice retention rules), delete everything else and clearly explain the narrower retention to the user — do not use this as a blanket excuse to retain more than necessary (Necessity principle, Art. 6, III).
- If your CRM, email platform, or analytics tool are third-party vendors acting as **processors**, review your contracts/DPAs now to confirm they support deletion-on-instruction — this is a good moment to close any gaps.
- If the analytics tool only holds pseudonymous/aggregated data where the individual cannot reasonably be re-identified, it may already fall outside the definition of "personal data" (Art. 5, III) — but if any identifier (user ID, device ID, IP) ties back to the individual, it is in scope and must be deleted or anonymised.
