NEW LEVEL A CRITERIA (4 criteria):
- None of the new criteria are Level A only in this batch. Two are Level A:

Actually, the correct breakdown from the WCAG 2.2 specification is:

LEVEL A (new in 2.2):
  - SC 3.2.6 Consistent Help
  - SC 3.3.7 Redundant Entry

LEVEL AA (new in 2.2):
  - SC 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)
  - SC 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) [Level AAA - not required for AA]
  - SC 2.4.13 Focus Appearance [Level AAA - not required for AA]
  - SC 2.5.7 Dragging Movements
  - SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)
  - SC 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum)
  - SC 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced) [Level AAA - not required for AA]

LEVEL AAA (not required for AA conformance):
  - SC 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced)
  - SC 2.4.13 Focus Appearance
  - SC 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced)


CRITERIA REQUIRED FOR WCAG 2.2 AA CONFORMANCE (that were not in WCAG 2.1 AA)
=============================================================================

The new criteria you must meet to upgrade from WCAG 2.1 AA to WCAG 2.2 AA are:

  Level A (2 new):
    1. SC 3.2.6 Consistent Help
    2. SC 3.3.7 Redundant Entry

  Level AA (4 new):
    3. SC 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)
    4. SC 2.5.7 Dragging Movements
    5. SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)
    6. SC 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum)

Total: 6 new success criteria to add to your conformance claim.


DETAILED BREAKDOWN OF EACH NEW CRITERION
=========================================

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
1. SC 3.2.6 - Consistent Help [Level A | POUR: Understandable]
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

REQUIREMENT:
If a web page provides any of the following help mechanisms — human contact details,
human contact mechanisms (e.g., live chat), self-help options, or fully automated
contact mechanisms (e.g., chatbot) — and those mechanisms are repeated across multiple
pages within a set of web pages, they must appear in the same relative order in the
page content as they do on other pages, unless a change is initiated by the user.

This criterion is about location consistency, not the presence of help. You are not
required to provide help — but if you do provide it consistently, it must appear in a
predictable location.

CONCRETE FAILURE EXAMPLE:
A multi-page e-commerce checkout flow includes a "Chat with Support" button. On the
product page and cart page, this button appears in the footer. On the payment page,
the same "Chat with Support" button is moved to the top of the sidebar. A user with
cognitive disabilities who learned to find support in the footer now cannot locate it
when they need help most (during payment). This is a failure of SC 3.2.6.

ADDITIONAL FAILURE EXAMPLE:
A software documentation site has a "Contact Support" link in the top navigation on
all pages except the error pages, where it is moved into the body content. This
inconsistency in ordering/position fails SC 3.2.6.

HOW TO FIX:
- Audit all pages within each "set of web pages" (typically a website or web app) for
  help mechanism placement.
- Use a consistent, templated layout (e.g., footer, persistent header widget) that
  ensures help links/buttons always appear in the same visual and DOM order.
- If you use a chat widget that floats in the same corner on every page, that is
  generally acceptable as consistent placement.
- Document your help placement pattern and include it in your design system/style guide.


-----------------------------------------------------------------------
2. SC 3.3.7 - Redundant Entry [Level A | POUR: Understandable]
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

REQUIREMENT:
Information previously entered by or provided to the user that is required again in
the same process must either be auto-populated or available for the user to select,
unless re-entering the information is essential, the information is a security measure
(e.g., password confirmation), or the information is no longer valid.

A "process" is a series of steps that must be completed in sequence to accomplish a
goal (e.g., registration, checkout, a multi-step form).

CONCRETE FAILURE EXAMPLE:
A job application portal has a 5-step form. In Step 1, the user enters their name,
email, and phone number. In Step 4 ("Review and Submit"), the form asks the user to
re-enter their email address to confirm. Because email confirmation in this context is
not security-critical and the original entry is still valid, requiring the user to
type it again is a failure of SC 3.3.7.

ADDITIONAL FAILURE EXAMPLE:
An insurance quote form asks for the user's date of birth on page 1. On page 3, it
asks for their age (which is derivable from DOB). This is redundant entry because the
system could calculate age from the previously provided DOB.

ADDITIONAL FAILURE EXAMPLE:
A shipping checkout form collects a billing address. The shipping address form that
follows does not offer a "Same as billing address" checkbox or auto-populate the
fields, forcing all users who have the same shipping and billing address to type it
again manually.

HOW TO FIX:
- Store user-entered data in session/state and auto-populate fields where the same
  information is required in subsequent steps.
- Provide a "Same as [previous entry]" checkbox or equivalent mechanism wherever
  address or identity information may be reused.
- For truly redundant fields that serve no security or validation purpose, remove them.
- Where re-entry is genuinely required (e.g., new password + confirm password for
  security), document the exception and ensure it is essential.


-----------------------------------------------------------------------
3. SC 2.4.11 - Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) [Level AA | POUR: Operable]
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

REQUIREMENT:
When a user interface component receives keyboard focus, it must not be entirely
hidden by author-created content. The component may be partially obscured, but the
focused component must not be completely hidden.

This criterion addresses a common failure pattern where sticky headers, cookie banners,
chat widgets, or fixed-position footers cover the focused element, making it invisible
to keyboard users.

Note: The enhanced version (SC 2.4.12, Level AAA) requires that no part of the focused
component is hidden — this stricter version is not required for AA.

CONCRETE FAILURE EXAMPLE:
A webpage has a sticky navigation bar fixed at the top of the viewport (height: 64px).
When a keyboard user tabs through a long page, the focused link near the top of the
page content scrolls behind the sticky header and is completely invisible on screen.
The user cannot see which element has focus, making the page effectively unusable with
a keyboard. This is a failure of SC 2.4.11.

ADDITIONAL FAILURE EXAMPLE:
A GDPR cookie consent banner fixed at the bottom of the viewport covers a row of
action buttons. When the user tabs to those buttons, they receive focus (shown by
browser focus ring) but are entirely hidden behind the cookie banner. The user cannot
see or interact with the focused button.

ADDITIONAL FAILURE EXAMPLE:
A live chat widget pinned to the bottom-right corner obscures the "Submit" button of
a form positioned at the bottom of the page. When the Submit button receives focus,
it is completely behind the chat widget.

HOW TO FIX:
- Use scroll-margin-top (or scroll-padding-top on the scroll container) set to at
  least the height of any sticky header, so focused elements scroll into view below
  the fixed element.
  Example CSS: html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; } /* matches sticky header height */
- Ensure fixed/sticky elements have z-index management so that focused interactive
  elements are not permanently covered.
- Test every focusable element on the page with a keyboard (Tab/Shift+Tab) to verify
  the focus indicator is visible.
- Consider reducing the size or dismissing non-essential overlays (chat widgets,
  cookie banners) after user interaction.


-----------------------------------------------------------------------
4. SC 2.5.7 - Dragging Movements [Level AA | POUR: Operable]
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

REQUIREMENT:
All functionality that uses a dragging movement for operation must be achievable by
a single pointer without dragging, unless dragging is essential or the dragging
functionality is determined by the user agent and not modified by the author.

This helps users who cannot perform dragging gestures (e.g., people with motor
disabilities, tremors, or who use switch access or voice control).

"Dragging movement" means clicking/touching, holding, and moving to another location
before releasing. "Single pointer" means interaction with one point of contact (finger,
mouse, stylus).

CONCRETE FAILURE EXAMPLE:
A Kanban board requires users to drag task cards from one column to another to change
their status. There is no alternative mechanism (e.g., a dropdown or button on the
card) to change the task's column/status without dragging. A user with limited motor
control who cannot reliably perform a click-hold-drag action cannot use this feature.
This is a failure of SC 2.5.7.

ADDITIONAL FAILURE EXAMPLE:
A volume slider control can only be adjusted by clicking and dragging the thumb along
the track. There are no increment/decrement buttons, no click-on-track behavior to
jump to a position, and no keyboard support that satisfies this pointer-specific
criterion. (Note: lack of keyboard support would also fail SC 2.1.1.)

ADDITIONAL FAILURE EXAMPLE:
An image cropping tool requires the user to drag handles to set crop boundaries, with
no numeric input fields or alternative single-click mechanism to set crop dimensions.

HOW TO FIX:
- For every drag interaction, provide at least one non-drag alternative using a single
  pointer action (click, tap):
    * Kanban: Add a "Move to..." dropdown menu or context menu on each card.
    * Sliders: Add +/- buttons flanking the slider, or allow clicking on the track.
    * Sortable lists: Add "Move up" / "Move down" buttons on each list item.
    * Resizable panels: Add a numeric input or preset size buttons as alternatives.
- The alternative does not have to be visually prominent by default, but must be
  available and functional for all users.


-----------------------------------------------------------------------
5. SC 2.5.8 - Target Size (Minimum) [Level AA | POUR: Operable]
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

REQUIREMENT:
The size of the target for pointer inputs must be at least 24x24 CSS pixels, except
where:
  a) The target offset is sufficient: The target is smaller than 24x24 but there is
     enough space around it so that a 24px circle centered on the target does not
     intersect any adjacent target or the bounding box of any adjacent target's
     spacing.
  b) Equivalent: The same function can be achieved through a different control on the
     same page that meets the 24x24 minimum.
  c) Inline: The target is in a sentence or its size is otherwise constrained to the
     line-height of non-target text.
  d) User agent: The target size and spacing is determined by the user agent and not
     modified by the author.
  e) Essential: A particular presentation of the target is essential or is legally
     required.

NOTE: The enhanced version (SC 2.5.5, Level AAA) requires 44x44 CSS pixels — this
was already in WCAG 2.1 but at AAA. The new SC 2.5.8 establishes a minimum (lower)
bar at Level AA.

CONCRETE FAILURE EXAMPLE:
A web application has a data table where each row has an "Edit" icon button (pencil
icon) that is only 16x16 CSS pixels in size. Adjacent rows also have 16x16 buttons
with no spacing between them. A user with a motor disability using a touchscreen or
imprecise pointer cannot reliably tap the correct button without accidentally activating
an adjacent row's button. This fails SC 2.5.8.

ADDITIONAL FAILURE EXAMPLE:
A cookie preferences dialog has 12 toggle switches rendered at 20x12 CSS pixels each,
stacked with 2px gaps between them. Neither the targets themselves (20x12 < 24x24)
nor their spacing provides a sufficient 24px "buffer zone." This fails SC 2.5.8.

ADDITIONAL FAILURE EXAMPLE:
A pagination component renders page number links as small inline numbers (18x18 CSS
pixels) with only 4px gaps between them. Because they are not inline in a block of
text (they are a nav component), the inline exception does not apply. This fails SC
2.5.8.

HOW TO FIX:
- Set minimum dimensions: button { min-width: 24px; min-height: 24px; }
- For icon-only buttons, add padding to increase the clickable/tappable area even if
  the visual icon remains small: button { padding: 10px; } (16px icon + 8px padding
  each side = 32x32 touch target)
- Use the "offset/spacing" approach: if a target is smaller than 24px, ensure the
  surrounding non-interactive space creates a 24px buffer (calculated using the
  overlapping-circles method described in the Understanding document).
- Audit with browser DevTools: inspect computed sizes and add visual outlines to
  confirm target dimensions.
- Pay special attention to mobile/touch UI components, icon buttons in toolbars,
  social share buttons, and form controls.


-----------------------------------------------------------------------
6. SC 3.3.8 - Accessible Authentication (Minimum) [Level AA | POUR: Understandable]
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

REQUIREMENT:
A cognitive function test (such as remembering a password, solving a puzzle, or
recognizing images) must not be required for any step in an authentication process
unless at least one of the following is true:
  a) Alternative: Another authentication method is available that does not rely on a
     cognitive function test.
  b) Mechanism: A mechanism is available to assist the user in completing the cognitive
     function test (e.g., a password manager is not blocked; copy-paste is allowed).
  c) Object recognition: The cognitive function test is to recognize objects (e.g.,
     "click all images containing a fire hydrant" CAPTCHAs that rely on object
     recognition, which is considered less cognitively demanding than memory or
     transcription).
  d) Personal content: The cognitive function test is to identify non-text content the
     user provided to the website (e.g., "select the image you chose as your security
     image").

A "cognitive function test" means any test that requires the user to remember,
manipulate, or transcribe information. Transcribing distorted text (classic CAPTCHA)
and solving math puzzles are cognitive function tests.

The enhanced version (SC 3.3.9, Level AAA) removes exceptions (c) and (d), also
prohibiting object recognition and personal content tests — not required for AA.

CONCRETE FAILURE EXAMPLE:
A login form includes a reCAPTCHA v2 "I'm not a robot" challenge that, when triggered,
presents a grid of images and asks the user to "select all squares with traffic lights."
If this is the only authentication pathway and there is no alternative login method
(e.g., magic link, passkey, SSO), this fails SC 3.3.8 because:
  - The image recognition CAPTCHA is a cognitive function test.
  - No alternative non-cognitive-test authentication method exists.
  - No mechanism bypasses the CAPTCHA (e.g., audio alternative may satisfy the
    "mechanism" exception, but only if it genuinely works for users with cognitive
    disabilities — audio CAPTCHAs are often not accessible either).

ADDITIONAL FAILURE EXAMPLE:
A banking portal's two-factor authentication requires the user to answer a "security
question" chosen during registration (e.g., "What was the name of your first pet?").
This is a memory-based cognitive function test. If there is no alternative 2FA method
(SMS code, authenticator app, biometric) and no mechanism to look up the answer, this
fails SC 3.3.8.

ADDITIONAL FAILURE EXAMPLE:
A login form blocks pasting into the password field (via JavaScript preventDefault on
paste events). This prevents password manager autofill from functioning, effectively
forcing users to manually transcribe (and thus memorize) their password. The "mechanism"
exception (allowing password managers) is violated. This fails SC 3.3.8.

HOW TO FIX:
- Allow password managers to autofill: do not use autocomplete="off" on password
  fields; do not block paste events; do not use custom input fields that intercept
  clipboard access.
- Implement passkey (WebAuthn) authentication as an alternative — passkeys use
  biometric or PIN authentication and do not require cognitive function tests.
- If you use CAPTCHA, provide a robust audio alternative that is actually usable, or
  switch to invisible bot-detection solutions (reCAPTCHA v3 behavior-based, Cloudflare
  Turnstile, hCaptcha accessibility mode).
- For 2FA, offer TOTP authenticator apps or SMS codes in addition to security
  questions.


SUMMARY TABLE
=============

| SC       | Name                              | Level | Status in 2.2 | Action Required       |
|----------|-----------------------------------|-------|---------------|-----------------------|
| 4.1.1    | Parsing                           | A     | REMOVED       | Remove from checklist |
| 3.2.6    | Consistent Help                   | A     | NEW           | Must meet for AA      |
| 3.3.7    | Redundant Entry                   | A     | NEW           | Must meet for AA      |
| 2.4.11   | Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)      | AA    | NEW           | Must meet for AA      |
| 2.5.7    | Dragging Movements                | AA    | NEW           | Must meet for AA      |
| 2.5.8    | Target Size (Minimum)             | AA    | NEW           | Must meet for AA      |
| 3.3.8    | Accessible Authentication (Min)   | AA    | NEW           | Must meet for AA      |
| 2.4.12   | Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced)     | AAA   | NEW           | Optional (AAA only)   |
| 2.4.13   | Focus Appearance                  | AAA   | NEW           | Optional (AAA only)   |
| 3.3.9    | Accessible Authentication (Enh)   | AAA   | NEW           | Optional (AAA only)   |


RECOMMENDED UPGRADE PATH
=========================

1. AUDIT PHASE
   - Conduct a keyboard-only walkthrough of every page and workflow to identify
     focus obscurance issues (SC 2.4.11).
   - Measure all interactive targets for size compliance (SC 2.5.8) using DevTools.
   - Map all multi-step processes and document where previously entered data is
     re-requested (SC 3.3.7).
   - Inventory all draggable UI components and their alternative interactions (SC 2.5.7).
   - Review all authentication flows for cognitive function test dependencies (SC 3.3.8).
   - Document all help mechanisms and verify their placement consistency (SC 3.2.6).

2. REMEDIATION PHASE (recommended priority order)
   Priority 1 (High impact, often systemic):
     - SC 2.5.8: Target size — often requires a CSS/design system update.
     - SC 3.3.8: Accessible authentication — may require architectural changes.
     - SC 2.4.11: Focus obscurance — often a CSS scroll-padding fix.

   Priority 2 (Moderate effort, clear implementation):
     - SC 3.3.7: Redundant entry — requires form state management.
     - SC 2.5.7: Dragging — requires alternative interaction design per component.

   Priority 3 (Policy/template updates):
     - SC 3.2.6: Consistent help — usually a template/layout audit and fix.

3. DOCUMENTATION PHASE
   - Update your Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR/VPAT) to reference WCAG 2.2.
   - Update your accessibility statement to claim WCAG 2.2 AA (not 2.1 AA).
   - Remove SC 4.1.1 from your checklist or mark it as "Not applicable (removed in 2.2)".
   - Document any exceptions claimed under SC 2.5.8 (inline, essential, user agent).

4. TESTING PHASE
   - Retest with automated tools updated for WCAG 2.2 (axe-core 4.8+, Deque, WAVE).
   - Conduct manual testing with keyboard, screen reader, and touch device.
   - Include users with cognitive and motor disabilities in user testing where possible.


IMPORTANT NOTES ON BACKWARD COMPATIBILITY
==========================================

- WCAG 2.2 is fully backward compatible with WCAG 2.1 (except for the removal of
  SC 4.1.1). Every criterion you currently meet under WCAG 2.1 AA continues to apply.
- You do not need to re-test or re-document existing WCAG 2.1 criteria unless you
  have made changes to your site that might have introduced new issues.
- If your conformance claim references WCAG 2.1, you may update it to reference
  WCAG 2.2 once you have met all 6 new required success criteria and confirmed
  continued conformance with existing criteria.
- The WCAG 2.2 specification is available at: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/
- The "Understanding WCAG 2.2" document provides normative guidance and techniques
  for each SC: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/


END OF REPORT

✅Lists new Level A criteria in 2.2 (3.2.6 and 3.3.7) that also apply for AA conformance
✅Mentions SC 4.1.1 Parsing was removed in WCAG 2.2

WCAG 2.1 AA to WCAG 2.2 AA Upgrade: New Success Criteria
==========================================================
Date: 2026-05-16

WCAG 2.2 was published as a W3C Recommendation in October 2023. When upgrading
a conformance claim from WCAG 2.1 AA to WCAG 2.2 AA, you must meet the
following new success criteria (WCAG 2.2 removes 4.1.1 Parsing, which was
previously AA, so that one is gone, but the new additions at AA level are the
ones listed below).

Note: WCAG 2.2 adds nine new success criteria total across A, AA, and AAA
levels. The ones that apply to an AA conformance claim (i.e., all A and AA
criteria) are:

------------------------------------------------------------------------
NEW SUCCESS CRITERIA REQUIRED FOR WCAG 2.2 AA
------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. 2.4.11 - Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) [AA]
   -----------------------------------------------
   WHAT IT REQUIRES:
   When a user interface component receives keyboard focus, the component must
   not be entirely hidden by author-created content. At minimum, some part of
   the focused element must remain visible. The component does not need to be
   fully visible — partial visibility satisfies this criterion — but it cannot
   be completely covered.

   WHAT MIGHT FAIL:
   A website has a sticky header navigation bar fixed to the top of the page.
   When a user tabs through links on the page, the focused link scrolls up and
   becomes completely hidden behind the sticky header. The user cannot see which
   element has focus at all, causing complete loss of orientation for keyboard
   users.

2. 2.4.12 - Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) [AAA - NOT required for AA]
   NOTE: This is AAA, not required for AA conformance. Listed here for
   completeness but you do NOT need to meet this for a 2.2 AA claim.

3. 2.4.13 - Focus Appearance [AAA - NOT required for AA]
   NOTE: This is also AAA. Not required for AA conformance.

4. 2.5.7 - Dragging Movements [AA]
   ---------------------------------
   WHAT IT REQUIRES:
   All functionality that uses a dragging movement for operation must also be
   achievable by a single pointer (e.g., a click or tap) without dragging,
   unless dragging is essential. This ensures that users who have difficulty
   performing precise dragging actions (such as people with motor disabilities
   or tremors) can still access the functionality.

   WHAT MIGHT FAIL:
   A Kanban-style task management board requires users to drag cards from one
   column to another to change their status. There is no alternative way to
   move a card — no "Move to..." button, context menu, or keyboard shortcut.
   Users who cannot perform a click-and-drag gesture (e.g., someone using a
   switch device or someone with hand tremors) are completely unable to change
   task status.

5. 2.5.8 - Target Size (Minimum) [AA]
   -------------------------------------
   WHAT IT REQUIRES:
   The size of the target (the clickable/tappable area) for pointer inputs must
   be at least 24x24 CSS pixels, OR there must be sufficient spacing around
   smaller targets such that the total area (target plus spacing) meets the
   24x24 CSS pixel minimum. Inline targets within text (like hyperlinks in a
   paragraph) are exempt, as are targets where the size is determined by the
   user agent and not modified by the author, and where the size is essential
   to the information being conveyed.

   WHAT MIGHT FAIL:
   A mobile-friendly website has a row of small social media icon links in the
   footer. Each icon is rendered at 16x16 CSS pixels with only 2px of margin
   between them. Because neither the icon itself nor the surrounding spacing
   meets the 24x24 CSS pixel minimum, users with motor impairments, large
   fingers, or hand tremors are likely to miss or accidentally activate the
   wrong link.

6. 3.2.6 - Consistent Help [A]
   -----------------------------
   WHAT IT REQUIRES:
   If a web page includes any of the following help mechanisms — human contact
   details, a human contact mechanism (e.g., a chat button), a self-help option
   (e.g., an FAQ or help center link), or a fully automated contact mechanism
   (e.g., a chatbot) — that mechanism must appear in the same relative location
   across multiple pages of the website when it appears on multiple pages.

   WHAT MIGHT FAIL:
   An e-commerce site displays a "Live Chat" button in the bottom-right corner
   on the homepage and product pages, but on the checkout page the Live Chat
   button is moved to the top-left corner of the header. Users with cognitive
   disabilities who rely on consistent page layout to find help cannot locate
   the chat button when they encounter difficulties at checkout, because it has
   moved from the location they learned to expect.

7. 3.3.7 - Redundant Entry [A]
   -----------------------------
   WHAT IT REQUIRES:
   Information previously entered by the user that is required again in the
   same process must either be auto-populated or available for the user to
   select. Users should not be required to re-enter the same information they
   have already provided in an earlier step of a multi-step process. Exceptions
   apply when re-entering the information is essential (e.g., password
   confirmation fields), when the information is no longer valid, or when
   re-entering is required for security reasons.

   WHAT MIGHT FAIL:
   An online insurance application asks the user to enter their full name,
   address, and date of birth on page 1 of a 5-page form. On page 4, the same
   form asks the user to enter their name and date of birth again as part of
   a "policy holder confirmation" section, without pre-filling these fields
   from the earlier entry. Users with cognitive disabilities, memory
   impairments, or motor difficulties are burdened by having to re-type
   identical information they already provided.

8. 3.3.8 - Accessible Authentication (Minimum) [AA]
   ---------------------------------------------------
   WHAT IT REQUIRES:
   A cognitive function test (such as remembering a password, solving a puzzle,
   or transcribing characters) must not be required for any step in an
   authentication process, UNLESS at least one of the following is true:
   (a) An alternative authentication method is available that does not rely on
       a cognitive function test;
   (b) A mechanism is available to assist the user in completing the cognitive
       function test (e.g., a password manager is not blocked, copy-paste is
       allowed for OTP codes);
   (c) The cognitive function test is to recognize objects (e.g., select all
       images with traffic lights);
   (d) The cognitive function test is to identify non-text content the user
       provided themselves (e.g., identifying a personal photo they uploaded).

   WHAT MIGHT FAIL:
   A banking website's login page uses a CAPTCHA that requires users to
   transcribe distorted text characters. No alternative authentication method
   is provided, and there is no audio alternative. The site also blocks
   password manager autofill (via autocomplete="off"). Users with cognitive
   disabilities such as dyslexia, or users with memory impairments who rely on
   password managers, are locked out of their accounts with no accessible
   alternative.

   A second example: A site requires users to mentally solve an arithmetic
   puzzle ("What is 14 + 27?") to log in, with no alternative method offered.
   This imposes a cognitive function test that users with dyscalculia or other
   cognitive impairments cannot reliably pass.

9. 3.3.9 - Accessible Authentication (Enhanced) [AAA - NOT required for AA]
   NOTE: This is AAA. Not required for AA conformance.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
SUMMARY TABLE: NEW AA CRITERIA REQUIRED FOR WCAG 2.2 AA CONFORMANCE
------------------------------------------------------------------------

SC       | Level | Short Name                        | Guideline
---------|-------|-----------------------------------|---------------------------
2.4.11   | AA    | Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)      | 2.4 Navigable
2.5.7    | AA    | Dragging Movements                | 2.5 Input Modalities
2.5.8    | AA    | Target Size (Minimum)             | 2.5 Input Modalities
3.2.6    | A     | Consistent Help                   | 3.2 Predictable
3.3.7    | A     | Redundant Entry                   | 3.3 Input Assistance
3.3.8    | AA    | Accessible Authentication (Min.)  | 3.3 Input Assistance

NOTE: WCAG 2.2 also removes the previous requirement for 4.1.1 Parsing (which
was AA in WCAG 2.1). You no longer need to satisfy that criterion under a
WCAG 2.2 AA claim.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
IMPORTANT CONSIDERATIONS FOR YOUR UPGRADE EFFORT
------------------------------------------------------------------------

- Focus Not Obscured (2.4.11) is especially relevant if your UI uses sticky
  headers, sticky footers, cookie consent banners, chat widgets, or any fixed-
  position overlapping content. Audit all fixed/sticky elements.

- Dragging Movements (2.5.7) requires reviewing any drag-and-drop interfaces:
  sliders, sortable lists, Kanban boards, map panning, carousels, and similar
  interactions all need pointer-based (non-drag) alternatives.

- Target Size (2.5.8) requires measuring interactive elements. Icon buttons,
  pagination links, close buttons on modals, and small form controls are
  common failure points. Note that inline text links in body copy are exempt.

- Consistent Help (3.2.6) only applies if you offer help mechanisms. If you
  do, audit their position across all page templates.

- Redundant Entry (3.3.7) requires a review of all multi-step forms, checkout
  flows, registration wizards, and application forms.

- Accessible Authentication (3.3.8) requires reviewing all login, registration,
  MFA, and account recovery flows. Ensure password managers are not blocked
  and that CAPTCHAs have accessible alternatives or are replaced with
  object-recognition or user-content-identification approaches.
Prompt: Our React app has a custom modal dialog. Review the code and identify all WCAG accessibility issues (missing role=dialog, no focus management, span used as label, no Escape key handler, etc.)

✅Identifies missing focus management — focus not moved into modal on open (SC 2.4.3)
✅Identifies no focus trap / keyboard users can Tab outside modal (SC 2.1.2)
✅Identifies span used instead of label for form inputs (SC 1.3.1)

WCAG Accessibility Audit — ProfileModal Component
=================================================
Auditor: WCAG Expert Review (WCAG 2.1 AA baseline)
Date: 2026-05-16

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
-----------------
The ProfileModal component contains 7 distinct WCAG violations spanning all four POUR
principles. Several issues are critical (Level A) and would prevent assistive-technology
users from operating the modal at all. None of the violations require complex remediation;
all can be fixed with correct ARIA attributes, semantic HTML, and a small amount of focus-
management JavaScript.

==========================================================================
ISSUE 1 — Missing ARIA Dialog Role and Required ARIA Attributes
==========================================================================
WCAG Success Criterion: 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A)
POUR Principle: Robust

What the violation is:
The outer modal container <div class="modal-content"> carries no role="dialog" attribute.
Screen readers therefore have no way to announce to the user that a dialog has opened, and
cannot apply their dialog-mode interaction model. WCAG 4.1.2 requires that all UI
components expose their role programmatically. A dialog without role="dialog" (or
role="alertdialog") is announced as a generic container, disorienting assistive-technology
users who cannot tell they are inside an interactive overlay.

Additionally, every ARIA dialog must be labelled via aria-labelledby (pointing at the
dialog's heading) or aria-label, so the dialog's accessible name is announced when focus
enters it. Neither attribute is present.

Required fix:
  <div class="modal-content" role="dialog" aria-modal="true" aria-labelledby="modal-title">
  <h2 id="modal-title">Edit Profile</h2>

The aria-modal="true" attribute tells supporting browsers and screen readers that content
behind the dialog is inert, which is essential for browsers that do not natively support
inert. Note: aria-modal alone is not sufficient — see Issue 2 for focus trapping.

==========================================================================
ISSUE 2 — No Focus Trap Inside the Modal
==========================================================================
WCAG Success Criterion: 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap (Level A) — inverse obligation
                        2.1.1 Keyboard (Level A)
POUR Principle: Operable

What the violation is:
2.1.1 requires that all functionality be operable via keyboard. 2.1.2 requires that
keyboard focus not become trapped in a component in a way that prevents the user from
leaving — but the complementary obligation is that while a modal is open, focus must be
contained within it (ARIA Authoring Practices Guide §3.8 Dialog Pattern). Without a focus
trap, a keyboard user who tabs past the last focusable element in the modal will move focus
into the obscured background page. Because the background content is not made inert, they
can interact with page controls behind the modal, which is both a functional failure and a
disorienting experience. The WAI-ARIA APG Dialog Pattern, cited as a normative technique
for WCAG 2.1, mandates focus confinement.

Required fix (React hook):

  import { useEffect, useRef } from 'react';

  function useFocusTrap(ref, isActive) {
    useEffect(() => {
      if (!isActive) return;
      const focusable = ref.current?.querySelectorAll(
        'a[href], button:not([disabled]), textarea, input, select, [tabindex]:not([tabindex="-1"])'
      );
      const first = focusable?.[0];
      const last = focusable?.[focusable.length - 1];

      function handleKeyDown(e) {
        if (e.key !== 'Tab') return;
        if (e.shiftKey) {
          if (document.activeElement === first) { e.preventDefault(); last.focus(); }
        } else {
          if (document.activeElement === last) { e.preventDefault(); first.focus(); }
        }
      }
      document.addEventListener('keydown', handleKeyDown);
      first?.focus(); // move focus into dialog on open (see Issue 3)
      return () => document.removeEventListener('keydown', handleKeyDown);
    }, [isActive]);
  }

==========================================================================
ISSUE 3 — Focus Not Moved Into the Dialog on Open
==========================================================================
WCAG Success Criterion: 2.4.3 Focus Order (Level A)
POUR Principle: Operable

What the violation is:
When a modal opens, focus must be programmatically moved into the dialog. The current
implementation renders the modal into the DOM but leaves focus wherever it was (typically
on the "Edit Profile" trigger button in the background). A screen-reader user will hear
nothing change; a keyboard user must Tab many times to reach the modal content.
WCAG 2.4.3 requires that focus order preserve meaning and operability. APG Dialog Pattern
specifies that focus should be set to the first focusable element (or the dialog container
itself) immediately upon open.

Required fix:
Move focus to the first interactive element (or the dialog div) in the useEffect hook
shown in Issue 2 (first?.focus()). Also store the triggering element so focus can be
restored on close (Issue 4).

==========================================================================
ISSUE 4 — Focus Not Returned to Trigger on Close
==========================================================================
WCAG Success Criterion: 2.4.3 Focus Order (Level A)
POUR Principle: Operable

What the violation is:
When the modal closes, focus vanishes (typically moves to <body>). The user loses their
place in the page entirely. This is a well-established failure of 2.4.3 and is explicitly
called out in the ARIA APG Dialog Pattern: "When the dialog closes, focus returns to the
element that invoked the dialog."

Required fix:

  // Before opening the modal, capture the trigger
  const triggerRef = useRef(null);

  function handleOpen() {
    triggerRef.current = document.activeElement;
    setIsOpen(true);
  }

  function handleClose() {
    setIsOpen(false);
    triggerRef.current?.focus();
  }

==========================================================================
ISSUE 5 — Form Inputs Have No Programmatic Labels
==========================================================================
WCAG Success Criterion: 1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)
                        1.1.1 Non-text Content (Level A) — for placeholder-as-label pattern
                        2.4.6 Headings and Labels (Level AA)
POUR Principle: Perceivable, Operable

What the violation is:
Both form fields use a <span> as a visual label instead of a <label> element. A <span> has
no programmatic association with its input. When a screen reader focuses the input, it reads
only the placeholder text (if anything), not the field label. Placeholder text is
insufficient as a label for three additional reasons:
  (a) it disappears once the user starts typing, removing the visible label (failure of
      1.3.1 and 2.4.6 for sighted users with cognitive disabilities);
  (b) placeholder contrast is typically below 4.5:1, failing 1.4.3 (see Issue 6);
  (c) some screen readers do not consistently announce placeholder as the accessible name.

WCAG 1.3.1 requires that information conveyed visually (here, which field is which) be
programmatically determinable. The correct pattern is an explicit <label for="..."> or
wrapping label element.

Required fix:

  <div>
    <label htmlFor="full-name">Full Name</label>
    <input id="full-name" type="text" placeholder="Enter your name" />
  </div>
  <div>
    <label htmlFor="email">Email</label>
    <input id="email" type="email" placeholder="Enter email" />
  </div>

==========================================================================
ISSUE 6 — No Escape Key Handler to Close the Dialog
==========================================================================
WCAG Success Criterion: 2.1.1 Keyboard (Level A)
POUR Principle: Operable

What the violation is:
The ARIA Authoring Practices Guide Dialog Pattern (a normative technique for satisfying
WCAG 2.1.1) specifies that pressing Escape must close the dialog. The current implementation
provides no keyboard handler for the Escape key. Keyboard-only users must Tab to the Cancel
button and activate it — a longer path — and users who expect Escape to dismiss the overlay
(an established, cross-platform convention) have no way to do so. This is a failure of the
keyboard operability requirement.

Required fix:

  useEffect(() => {
    function onKeyDown(e) {
      if (e.key === 'Escape') onClose();
    }
    if (isOpen) document.addEventListener('keydown', onKeyDown);
    return () => document.removeEventListener('keydown', onKeyDown);
  }, [isOpen, onClose]);

==========================================================================
ISSUE 7 — Background Content Not Made Inert
==========================================================================
WCAG Success Criterion: 1.3.1 Info and Relationships (Level A)
                        4.1.3 Status Messages (Level AA) — secondary
POUR Principle: Perceivable, Robust

What the violation is:
When a modal is open, background page content should be hidden from the accessibility tree
so screen-reader users navigating with virtual cursor or browse mode cannot wander into
content that is visually obscured. aria-modal="true" signals inertness to some browsers but
is not universally honoured. The current component neither sets inert on the root, nor uses
aria-hidden="true" on background containers. Screen-reader users using virtual cursor can
read background content, which conflicts with the visual design intent and exposes
potentially confusing or misleading content relationships (1.3.1 failure).

Required fix (React approach):

  useEffect(() => {
    const appRoot = document.getElementById('root'); // or your app root
    if (isOpen) {
      appRoot.setAttribute('inert', '');
      appRoot.setAttribute('aria-hidden', 'true');
    } else {
      appRoot.removeAttribute('inert');
      appRoot.removeAttribute('aria-hidden');
    }
    return () => {
      appRoot.removeAttribute('inert');
      appRoot.removeAttribute('aria-hidden');
    };
  }, [isOpen]);

Note: The modal element itself must NOT be a descendant of the inert/aria-hidden root, or
it will be hidden from AT as well. Render the modal via a React Portal into document.body.

==========================================================================
COMPLETE CORRECTED COMPONENT
==========================================================================

import { useEffect, useRef } from 'react';
import { createPortal } from 'react-dom';

function ProfileModal({ isOpen, onClose, triggerRef }) {
  const dialogRef = useRef(null);

  // Focus trap + initial focus
  useEffect(() => {
    if (!isOpen || !dialogRef.current) return;

    const focusableSelectors =
      'a[href], button:not([disabled]), textarea, input, select, [tabindex]:not([tabindex="-1"])';
    const focusableElements = dialogRef.current.querySelectorAll(focusableSelectors);
    const firstEl = focusableElements[0];
    const lastEl = focusableElements[focusableElements.length - 1];

    firstEl?.focus();

    function handleTabKey(e) {
      if (e.key !== 'Tab') return;
      if (e.shiftKey) {
        if (document.activeElement === firstEl) {
          e.preventDefault();
          lastEl.focus();
        }
      } else {
        if (document.activeElement === lastEl) {
          e.preventDefault();
          firstEl.focus();
        }
      }
    }

    function handleEscape(e) {
      if (e.key === 'Escape') onClose();
    }

    document.addEventListener('keydown', handleTabKey);
    document.addEventListener('keydown', handleEscape);
    return () => {
      document.removeEventListener('keydown', handleTabKey);
      document.removeEventListener('keydown', handleEscape);
    };
  }, [isOpen, onClose]);

  // Return focus to trigger on close
  useEffect(() => {
    if (!isOpen && triggerRef?.current) {
      triggerRef.current.focus();
    }
  }, [isOpen, triggerRef]);

  // Make background inert
  useEffect(() => {
    const appRoot = document.getElementById('root');
    if (!appRoot) return;
    if (isOpen) {
      appRoot.setAttribute('inert', '');
      appRoot.setAttribute('aria-hidden', 'true');
    } else {
      appRoot.removeAttribute('inert');
      appRoot.removeAttribute('aria-hidden');
    }
    return () => {
      appRoot.removeAttribute('inert');
      appRoot.removeAttribute('aria-hidden');
    };
  }, [isOpen]);

  if (!isOpen) return null;

  return createPortal(
    // Overlay: clicking it closes the dialog; stop propagation inside the dialog
    <div
      className="modal-overlay"
      onClick={onClose}
      aria-hidden="true" /* overlay itself is decorative */
    >
      <div
        ref={dialogRef}
        className="modal-content"
        role="dialog"
        aria-modal="true"
        aria-labelledby="modal-title"
        onClick={(e) => e.stopPropagation()} /* prevent overlay click from firing inside */
      >
        <h2 id="modal-title">Edit Profile</h2>
        <form>
          <div>
            <label htmlFor="full-name">Full Name</label>
            <input
              id="full-name"
              type="text"
              placeholder="Enter your name"
              autoComplete="name"
            />
          </div>
          <div>
            <label htmlFor="email">Email</label>
            <input
              id="email"
              type="email"
              placeholder="Enter email"
              autoComplete="email"
            />
          </div>
          <div className="buttons">
            <button type="button" onClick={onClose}>
              Cancel
            </button>
            <button type="submit">Save Changes</button>
          </div>
        </form>
      </div>
    </div>,
    document.body
  );
}

/* Usage in parent — capture trigger ref for focus restoration: */
function ProfilePage() {
  const [isOpen, setIsOpen] = React.useState(false);
  const triggerRef = useRef(null);

  return (
    <>
      <button ref={triggerRef} onClick={() => setIsOpen(true)}>
        Edit Profile
      </button>
      <ProfileModal
        isOpen={isOpen}
        onClose={() => setIsOpen(false)}
        triggerRef={triggerRef}
      />
    </>
  );
}

| 2 | No focus trap                      | 2.1.1/2.1.2 | A     | Operable    |
| 3 | Focus not moved to dialog on open  | 2.4.3       | A     | Operable    |
| 4 | Focus not restored to trigger      | 2.4.3       | A     | Operable    |
| 5 | Inputs lack programmatic labels    | 1.3.1/2.4.6 | A/AA  | Perceivable |

All 7 issues are resolved in the corrected component above. Six of the seven violations
are Level A — the most severe conformance level — meaning the modal would fail even a
minimum WCAG 2.1 Level A audit in its original form.

Additional recommended enhancement (not a WCAG violation but best practice):
- Add autoComplete="name" and autoComplete="email" on the inputs to support SC 1.3.5
  Identify Input Purpose (Level AA, WCAG 2.1) for users of autofill tools.
  (Included in the corrected code above.)

WCAG Accessibility Issues in ProfileModal Component
====================================================

The following WCAG 2.1 accessibility issues were identified in the ProfileModal component:

---

1. MISSING ARIA ROLE FOR DIALOG (WCAG 4.1.2 - Name, Role, Value)
   The modal container div lacks role="dialog" (or role="alertdialog"). Without this,
   assistive technologies like screen readers will not announce this as a dialog,
   and users will have no indication they are in a modal context.
   Fix: Add role="dialog" and aria-modal="true" to the modal-content div.

2. MISSING ACCESSIBLE NAME FOR THE DIALOG (WCAG 4.1.2 - Name, Role, Value)
   The dialog has no aria-labelledby or aria-label attribute to provide an accessible
   name. Screen readers need to announce the purpose of the dialog when it receives
   focus.
   Fix: Add aria-labelledby pointing to the h2 element's id
   (e.g., <h2 id="modal-title">Edit Profile</h2> and aria-labelledby="modal-title").

3. NO FOCUS MANAGEMENT / FOCUS TRAP (WCAG 2.1.2 - No Keyboard Trap; 2.4.3 - Focus Order)
   When the modal opens, focus is not programmatically moved into the modal. Users
   navigating by keyboard will remain focused on whatever element was active before,
   making it difficult or impossible to interact with the modal. Additionally, there
   is no focus trap, so Tab/Shift+Tab can cycle focus outside the modal while it is
   open, which is disorienting.
   Fix: On open, use useEffect and useRef to move focus to the first focusable element
   (or the modal container itself). Implement a focus trap that constrains keyboard
   navigation within the modal while it is open.

4. MISSING RETURN OF FOCUS ON CLOSE (WCAG 2.4.3 - Focus Order)
   When the modal closes, focus is not returned to the element that triggered it
   (the "Edit Profile" button). Screen reader and keyboard users will lose their
   place in the page.
   Fix: Store a reference to the trigger element before opening the modal and restore
   focus to it when the modal closes.

5. NO KEYBOARD HANDLER FOR ESCAPE KEY (WCAG 2.1.1 - Keyboard)
   The modal provides no way to close it via the keyboard (specifically the Escape
   key, which is the standard pattern for dismissing dialogs per ARIA Authoring
   Practices Guide). Keyboard-only users cannot dismiss the modal without clicking
   outside it or pressing Cancel.
   Fix: Add a keydown event listener (e.g., onKeyDown on the dialog) that calls
   onClose when the Escape key is pressed.

6. CLICK-TO-CLOSE OVERLAY HAS NO KEYBOARD EQUIVALENT (WCAG 2.1.1 - Keyboard)
   The modal-overlay div uses onClick={onClose} to close the modal when users click
   outside the content area. This is a mouse-only interaction; keyboard users cannot
   replicate this behavior by tabbing to the overlay. Divs are not natively focusable
   or activatable.
   Fix: Either remove this pattern and rely on an explicit close button + Escape key,
   or add role="button", tabIndex={0}, and a corresponding onKeyDown handler to make
   the overlay keyboard-accessible.

7. FORM INPUTS USE <span> INSTEAD OF <label> (WCAG 1.3.1 - Info and Relationships; 1.3.5 - Identify Input Purpose; 2.4.6 - Headings and Labels)
   The "Full Name" and "Email" field labels are plain <span> elements, which are not
   programmatically associated with their corresponding inputs. Screen readers will
   not announce the label when the input is focused, leaving users without context
   for what to type.
   Fix: Replace <span> with <label> and use either a for/htmlFor attribute matching
   each input's id, or wrap the input inside the label element.

8. PLACEHOLDER TEXT USED AS THE ONLY LABEL ALTERNATIVE (WCAG 1.3.1; 3.3.2 - Labels or Instructions)
   While placeholders are present ("Enter your name", "Enter email"), placeholder
   text disappears as soon as users begin typing and has insufficient color contrast
   in many browsers by default. Placeholders must never be used as a substitute for
   visible, persistent labels.
   Fix: Keep labels (see issue 7) as the primary label; treat placeholder as optional
   hint text only.

9. NO VISIBLE CLOSE BUTTON (WCAG 2.4.3 - Focus Order; 2.1.1 - Keyboard; ARIA Dialog Pattern)
   There is no dedicated close/dismiss button (typically an "X" button) in the modal
   header. The only way to close the modal is the Cancel button or clicking outside.
   ARIA Authoring Practices recommend a visible close button within the dialog.
   Fix: Add a close button (e.g., an X icon button) in the modal header with an
   accessible name like aria-label="Close dialog".

10. INSUFFICIENT COLOR CONTRAST CANNOT BE VERIFIED WITHOUT STYLES (WCAG 1.4.3 - Contrast Minimum)
    The code provides no color information. If the chosen text colors, background
    colors, or placeholder colors do not meet the 4.5:1 ratio (normal text) or 3:1
    (large text / UI components), this will be a WCAG failure.
    Fix: Audit CSS for all text/background color pairings and ensure they meet minimum
    contrast ratios. Placeholder text typically needs special attention.

11. FORM HAS NO SUBMIT HANDLER / ERROR HANDLING (WCAG 3.3.1 - Error Identification; 3.3.3 - Error Suggestion)
    The form lacks onSubmit handling and provides no visible or programmatic error
    messages if validation fails. Users with screen readers will not be informed of
    any errors after attempting to submit.
    Fix: Add onSubmit, perform validation, and surface error messages using
    aria-describedby or aria-live regions so that screen readers announce errors.

---

WCAG Legal Compliance Requirements: US, EU, and UK Jurisdictions
For a SaaS Company Serving Government and Private Sector Customers
Date: 2026-05-16
================================================================================

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
-----------------
As a SaaS company with customers in the US, EU, and UK spanning both government
agencies and private sector businesses, you face overlapping accessibility
mandates. The practical target that satisfies all jurisdictions is:

    WCAG 2.1 Level AA

This is the lowest common denominator that satisfies every applicable law
across your customer base. Where WCAG 2.2 is emerging as a requirement, the
good news is that WCAG 2.2 AA is a superset of WCAG 2.1 AA — achieving 2.2 AA
automatically satisfies 2.1 AA requirements. Targeting WCAG 2.2 AA now future-
proofs your product.

================================================================================
1. UNITED STATES — FEDERAL GOVERNMENT CUSTOMERS
================================================================================

Applicable Law: Section 508 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973
(29 U.S.C. § 794d), as amended and refreshed in 2018

Regulatory Body: U.S. Access Board; enforced via agency procurement and
the DOJ under the ADA for federally funded entities.

WCAG Requirement: WCAG 2.0 Level AA (incorporated by reference)

Details:
- The 2017 Section 508 "Refresh" (effective January 18, 2018) replaced the
  original 2001 technical standards by incorporating WCAG 2.0 Level AA by
  reference (36 C.F.R. Part 1194).
- The standard references WCAG 2.0, not 2.1 or 2.2 — however, the Access
  Board has signaled intent to update the reference to WCAG 2.1 or later.
  As of 2026, no formal rulemaking has finalized that update, so WCAG 2.0
  Level AA remains the legally referenced standard.
- In practice, agencies increasingly require or prefer WCAG 2.1 AA in
  solicitations and ACR (Accessibility Conformance Report / VPAT) reviews.
- Applies to: Electronic and Information Technology (EIT) procured by
  federal agencies. As a SaaS vendor to federal agencies, your product is
  subject to Section 508 review during procurement.
- You must provide an Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR) using the
  VPAT 2.x template (ITI VPAT) referencing WCAG 2.1 — this is the current
  industry-standard VPAT revision even though the regulation cites 2.0.

Key Deadlines:
- The 2017 refresh took effect January 18, 2018; no pending phase-in remains.
- Watch for a future rulemaking to update the WCAG reference — likely to 2.2.

Action Required: Achieve WCAG 2.0 Level AA (minimum legal), document via
VPAT 2.x referencing WCAG 2.1 Level AA for practical market access.

================================================================================
2. UNITED STATES — PRIVATE SECTOR CUSTOMERS
================================================================================

Applicable Laws:
  (a) Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), Titles II and III
      (42 U.S.C. §§ 12101 et seq.)
  (b) DOJ Final Rule on Web Accessibility for Title II entities
      (28 C.F.R. Part 35, published April 24, 2024)
  (c) Air Carrier Access Act (ACAA) — if applicable to airline customers
  (d) Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act — for federally funded recipients

WCAG Requirement:
  - Title II (state/local government): WCAG 2.1 Level AA — NOW MANDATED
  - Title III (private businesses): WCAG 2.1 Level AA — DOJ guidance and
    overwhelming court precedent treat 2.1 AA as the de facto standard;
    no formal final rule yet but litigation risk is high without it.

Title II DOJ Final Rule (April 2024) Details:
- The DOJ finalized a rule under ADA Title II (28 C.F.R. Part 35) requiring
  state and local government entities to conform to WCAG 2.1 Level AA for
  web content and mobile apps.
- Phase-in deadlines by entity size:
    * Population 50,000+: Compliance by April 24, 2026
    * Population 10,000–49,999: Compliance by April 26, 2027
    * Population under 10,000: Compliance by April 26, 2027
- NOTE: As of May 2026, the initial deadline for large entities has passed.
  If your customers include state/local government entities, they must now
  be compliant — and as their SaaS provider, your product must support their
  compliance.

Title III (Private Sector):
- No equivalent DOJ final rule exists for private businesses as of 2026, but
  the DOJ's 2022 guidance letter and consistent federal court decisions
  (9th Cir., 1st Cir., 11th Cir.) treat WCAG 2.1 AA as the appropriate
  technical standard.
- ADA Title III litigation volume remains high; WCAG 2.1 AA is the practical
  safe harbor even without a formal rule.
- State laws (e.g., California Unruh Act, New York state/city laws) may impose
  additional or parallel obligations.

Action Required: WCAG 2.1 Level AA is both the legal minimum for Title II
customers (mandated) and the prudent standard for all private sector customers.

================================================================================
3. EUROPEAN UNION — PUBLIC SECTOR CUSTOMERS
================================================================================

Applicable Law: EU Web Accessibility Directive
(Directive (EU) 2016/2102, "WAD")

Harmonized Standard: EN 301 549 V3.2.1 (2021) — incorporates WCAG 2.1 Level AA

WCAG Requirement: WCAG 2.1 Level AA (via EN 301 549)

Details:
- The WAD requires public sector bodies in all EU Member States to make their
  websites and mobile apps accessible in accordance with EN 301 549.
- EN 301 549 V3.2.1 (current as of 2026) incorporates WCAG 2.1 Level AA
  as its core web content requirements (Chapter 9 maps directly to WCAG 2.1).
- As a SaaS vendor to public sector bodies, your product must conform to
  EN 301 549 / WCAG 2.1 AA to be procurable under WAD-compliant procurement.
- Scope: All public sector bodies (government, universities, hospitals,
  publicly funded entities). Does NOT currently mandate private sector
  compliance under the WAD — that is covered by the EAA (see Section 4).
- Accessibility Statement: Required for public sector websites/apps; as a
  SaaS provider you may need to support your customers in generating these.

Key Deadlines: WAD has been in force since September 23, 2020 (websites) and
June 23, 2021 (mobile apps). All deadlines have passed.

EN 301 549 Updates: ETSI is expected to update EN 301 549 to reference
WCAG 2.2 in an upcoming revision. Monitor ETSI TC HF for publication.

Action Required: WCAG 2.1 Level AA conformance, documented via an
Accessibility Conformance Report against EN 301 549 V3.2.1.

================================================================================
4. EUROPEAN UNION — PRIVATE SECTOR CUSTOMERS
================================================================================

Applicable Law: European Accessibility Act
(Directive (EU) 2019/882, "EAA")

Harmonized Standard: EN 301 549 (same standard as WAD, incorporating WCAG 2.1 AA)

WCAG Requirement: WCAG 2.1 Level AA (via EN 301 549, per EAA)

Details:
- The EAA extends accessibility requirements to a broad range of private sector
  products and services, including: computers, smartphones, e-readers,
  e-commerce websites, banking services, e-books, audio/visual media services,
  transport services (ticketing/check-in), and — critically for SaaS —
  electronic communications services.
- "Services" in scope include any digital service provided to consumers in the
  EU. B2B SaaS is more nuanced: the EAA primarily targets B2C services, but
  if your SaaS is used to deliver services to end consumers (e.g., a customer-
  facing portal your EU enterprise customers use to serve their own customers),
  EAA obligations likely flow through.
- Member States were required to transpose the EAA into national law by
  June 28, 2022.

KEY DEADLINE — EAA COMPLIANCE DATE: June 28, 2025
- All covered products and services placed on the market or provided in the
  EU after June 28, 2025 must comply with EAA requirements.
- This deadline has now passed (as of May 2026). If your SaaS is in scope,
  EAA compliance is currently required.

Microenterprise Exemption:
- Microenterprises (fewer than 10 employees AND annual turnover/balance sheet
  not exceeding €2 million) providing services (not products) are exempt from
  the EAA. This exemption does not apply to products.

Disproportionate Burden Exception:
- Economic operators may claim an exemption if compliance would impose a
  disproportionate burden, but this requires documented assessment and is
  a narrow exception.

Action Required: Assess whether your SaaS services fall within EAA scope.
If yes (likely for B2C-facing functionality), WCAG 2.1 Level AA conformance
is required as of June 28, 2025.

5. UNITED KINGDOM
================================================================================

Applicable Laws:
  (a) Public Sector Bodies (Websites and Mobile Applications) Accessibility
      Regulations 2018 (SI 2018/952) — "UK PSBAR" — for public sector customers
  (b) Equality Act 2010 — for private sector customers
  (c) (Prospective) UK Accessibility Act / adoption of EAA equivalent —
      legislation in progress as of 2026

Public Sector (UK PSBAR):
WCAG Requirement: WCAG 2.1 Level AA

Details:
- UK PSBAR transposed the EU WAD into UK law pre-Brexit and was retained
  in domestic law post-Brexit.
- References EN 301 549 / WCAG 2.1 Level AA as the technical standard.
- Enforced by the Government Digital Service (GDS) / Cabinet Office.
- Applies to public sector bodies in England, Wales, Scotland (separate
  Scottish regulations apply), and Northern Ireland.
- Requires accessibility statements for covered websites and apps.
- Deadlines have passed: websites (September 23, 2020), mobile apps
  (June 23, 2021).

Private Sector (Equality Act 2010):
WCAG Requirement: No specific version mandated, but WCAG 2.1 AA is the
prevailing standard in UK case law and regulatory guidance.

Details:
- The Equality Act 2010 (sections 20–21) imposes a duty on service providers
  to make "reasonable adjustments" to ensure disabled people are not at a
  substantial disadvantage.
- The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) Code of Practice identifies
  website/digital accessibility as a key reasonable adjustment area.
- WCAG 2.1 Level AA is the de facto standard expected by UK courts and the
  EHRC, even without explicit statutory reference.
- UK has signaled intent to introduce EAA-equivalent private sector
  requirements post-Brexit, but as of May 2026 no equivalent legislation
  has been enacted for private businesses. Monitor UK government consultations.

Action Required: WCAG 2.1 Level AA for public sector customers (legally
mandated); WCAG 2.1 Level AA recommended for private sector customers
(Equality Act reasonable adjustment standard).

7. KEY DEADLINES SUMMARY (STATUS AS OF MAY 2026)
================================================================================

Date            | Jurisdiction | Event

Sep 23, 2020    | EU / UK      | WAD / PSBAR websites deadline — PASSED

8. PRACTICAL RECOMMENDATIONS
================================================================================

TARGET STANDARD: WCAG 2.2 Level AA
--------------------------------------
While WCAG 2.1 AA is the legal minimum across all jurisdictions, we strongly
recommend targeting WCAG 2.2 Level AA for the following reasons:

1. WCAG 2.2 is a superset of 2.1 — achieving 2.2 AA automatically satisfies
   all 2.1 AA requirements.
2. EN 301 549 is expected to reference WCAG 2.2 in its next revision,
   making 2.2 the future EU standard.
3. The US Access Board is expected to update Section 508 to reference WCAG 2.1
   or 2.2 in future rulemaking.
4. WCAG 2.2 adds 9 new success criteria (SC 2.4.11–2.4.13, 2.5.7–2.5.8,
   3.2.6, 3.3.7–3.3.9) that significantly improve mobile and cognitive
   accessibility — areas of increasing legal focus.
5. Future-proofing reduces remediation costs later.

STEP-BY-STEP COMPLIANCE ROADMAP:
----------------------------------

Step 1 — Baseline Audit (Immediate)
  - Conduct a WCAG 2.2 Level AA audit of your entire product (web + mobile).
  - Use automated tools (axe-core, Deque, WAVE) combined with manual testing
    and testing with assistive technology users (screen readers, keyboard-only,
    voice control).
  - Prioritize critical user journeys: sign-up, login, core product features,
    billing, support.

Step 2 — Remediation Backlog (0–6 months)
  - Triage findings by impact (blocker vs. moderate) and user flow criticality.
  - Fix blockers (keyboard traps, missing alt text, no focus indicators,
    inaccessible forms, missing error identification) first.
  - Establish a Definition of Done that includes accessibility for all new
    features going forward.

Step 3 — Documentation (Parallel)
  - Produce a VPAT 2.x (ACR) against WCAG 2.1 AA for US government procurement.
  - Produce an EN 301 549 V3.2.1 conformance report for EU/UK procurement.
  - Publish an Accessibility Statement on your website covering your current
    status, known issues, and contact mechanism for assistance requests.

Step 4 — Ongoing Testing Program
  - Integrate automated accessibility testing into your CI/CD pipeline.
  - Schedule quarterly manual audits covering assistive technology combinations:
    * NVDA + Firefox (Windows)
    * JAWS + Chrome (Windows)
    * VoiceOver + Safari (macOS/iOS)
    * TalkBack + Chrome (Android)
  - Update your ACR/VPAT at least annually or after major releases.

Step 5 — Legal Safeguards
  - Include accessibility commitments in customer contracts (SLA provisions).
  - Establish an accessibility feedback/complaint mechanism — required under
    WAD (EU) and PSBAR (UK), and best practice under ADA.
  - Document your remediation roadmap — demonstrates good faith under ADA
    undue hardship analysis and EAA disproportionate burden exception.

ARIA AND TECHNICAL NOTES:
  - Follow WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG) for all custom widgets.
  - Ensure all custom components have appropriate ARIA roles, states, and
    properties before relying on ARIA (use native HTML semantics first).
  - Test focus management for single-page application (SPA) route changes —
    a common failure in SaaS products.
  - Ensure all dynamic content updates are announced via live regions
    (aria-live, aria-atomic) appropriately.

================================================================================
9. SPECIFIC WCAG 2.2 SUCCESS CRITERIA TO PRIORITIZE (COMMON SAAS FAILURES)
================================================================================

The following SCs are frequently failed in SaaS applications and should receive
immediate attention during audit:

WCAG 2.1 (often failed in SaaS):
  1.4.3  Contrast (Minimum) — text/background color contrast ≥ 4.5:1
  1.4.4  Resize Text — usable at 200% zoom without loss of content
  1.4.11 Non-text Contrast — UI components/graphics ≥ 3:1 contrast ratio
  1.4.12 Text Spacing — content doesn't break with letter/line/word spacing overrides
  1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus — tooltips/popovers are dismissible, hoverable, persistent
  2.1.1  Keyboard — all functionality available via keyboard
  2.4.3  Focus Order — logical focus sequence in modals and overlays
  2.4.7  Focus Visible — keyboard focus indicator always visible
  3.3.1  Error Identification — errors described in text, not color alone
  3.3.2  Labels or Instructions — form inputs have visible labels
  4.1.2  Name, Role, Value — all UI components have accessible name/role/state
  4.1.3  Status Messages — non-focused status messages announced to screen readers

WCAG 2.2 additions (new requirements):
  2.4.11 Focus Appearance (Minimum) — focus indicator meets size and contrast requirements
  2.5.7  Dragging Movements — all drag-and-drop has a single-pointer alternative
  2.5.8  Target Size (Minimum) — interactive targets ≥ 24×24 CSS pixels
  3.2.6  Consistent Help — help mechanisms appear in consistent location
  3.3.7  Redundant Entry — previously entered information is auto-populated
  3.3.8  Accessible Authentication (Minimum) — no cognitive function test for login
         (this directly impacts CAPTCHA-based authentication flows)

before making final compliance determinations. This is not legal advice.

WCAG Version and Conformance Level Requirements by Region
For a SaaS company selling to government agencies and private sector businesses in the US, EU, and UK

=============================================================
UNITED STATES
=============================================================

Government Customers:
- Applicable Law: Section 508 of the Rehabilitation Act (29 U.S.C. § 794d), as revised in 2017
- Required Standard: WCAG 2.0, Level AA (incorporated by reference into the Revised Section 508 Standards)
- Who It Applies To: Federal agencies and any vendors/contractors providing electronic and information technology (EIT) to federal agencies
- Important Note: As a SaaS vendor selling to US federal agencies, your product must meet Section 508, which maps to WCAG 2.0 AA. Many states also have their own accessibility laws that mirror Section 508 or go further.
- Trend: The Access Board has signaled intent to update Section 508 to reference WCAG 2.1 or 2.2, but as of 2026 the legal baseline remains WCAG 2.0 AA.

Private Sector Customers:
- Applicable Law: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), Titles II and III
- Required Standard: No explicit WCAG version is written into the ADA statute, but the DOJ has issued rules (effective April 2026 for larger entities) requiring WCAG 2.1, Level AA for state and local government websites and web content (Title II).
- For Title III (private businesses open to the public): Courts and the DOJ consistently treat WCAG 2.1 AA as the de facto standard based on DOJ guidance and litigation outcomes.
- Practical Recommendation: Target WCAG 2.1 AA at a minimum for all US customers to satisfy both Section 508 and ADA obligations.

=============================================================
EUROPEAN UNION
=============================================================

Government Customers:
- Applicable Law: EU Web Accessibility Directive (Directive 2016/2102) and the European Accessibility Act (EAA, Directive 2019/882)
- Required Standard: EN 301 549 (the harmonized European standard), which currently references WCAG 2.1, Level AA
- Who It Applies To:
  * Web Accessibility Directive: Public sector bodies (government websites and mobile apps) — already in force
  * European Accessibility Act (EAA): Broader scope covering private sector products and services including SaaS, with compliance required by June 28, 2025
- Conformance Level: WCAG 2.1, Level AA (via EN 301 549 v3.2.1 or later)

Private Sector Customers:
- Applicable Law: European Accessibility Act (EAA), transposed into national law by each EU member state
- Required Standard: WCAG 2.1, Level AA (via EN 301 549)
- Effective Date: June 28, 2025 — private sector companies must comply
- Scope: The EAA covers a wide range of digital services and products, including SaaS platforms used by consumers and businesses
- Note: Individual EU member states may have additional national accessibility requirements that go beyond the EAA baseline.

=============================================================
UNITED KINGDOM
=============================================================

Government Customers:
- Applicable Law: Public Sector Bodies (Websites and Mobile Applications) Accessibility Regulations 2018 (SI 2018/952), implementing the EU Web Accessibility Directive post-Brexit
- Required Standard: WCAG 2.1, Level AA
- Who It Applies To: UK public sector bodies and vendors providing digital services to them
- Enforcement: The Government Digital Service (GDS) and Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) oversee compliance

Private Sector Customers:
- Applicable Law: Equality Act 2010 (the UK equivalent of the ADA)
- Required Standard: No explicit WCAG version mandated in statute, but WCAG 2.1 AA is the recognized benchmark used by courts and the EHRC
- Practical Recommendation: Target WCAG 2.1 AA to meet both public sector regulations and Equality Act obligations

=============================================================
SUMMARY TABLE
=============================================================

Region       | Customer Type    | Law/Regulation              | Required WCAG Version & Level
-------------|------------------|-----------------------------|------------------------------
US           | Government       | Section 508                 | WCAG 2.0, Level AA (minimum); WCAG 2.1 AA recommended
US           | Private Sector   | ADA (Titles II & III)       | WCAG 2.1, Level AA (de facto standard)
EU           | Government       | Web Accessibility Directive | WCAG 2.1, Level AA (via EN 301 549)
EU           | Private Sector   | European Accessibility Act  | WCAG 2.1, Level AA (via EN 301 549), effective June 28, 2025
UK           | Government       | Public Sector Bodies Regs   | WCAG 2.1, Level AA
UK           | Private Sector   | Equality Act 2010           | WCAG 2.1, Level AA (de facto standard)

=============================================================
PRACTICAL RECOMMENDATION
=============================================================

To meet legal compliance across all three regions and both customer types, you should target:

  >> WCAG 2.1, Level AA <<

This single standard satisfies:
- Section 508 (US federal government) — which legally requires WCAG 2.0 AA but WCAG 2.1 AA is a superset
- ADA requirements (US private sector)
- EN 301 549 / EU Web Accessibility Directive (EU government)
- European Accessibility Act (EU private sector)
- UK Public Sector Bodies Regulations (UK government)
- UK Equality Act (UK private sector)

Additional Considerations:
1. WCAG 2.2: Released in October 2023, WCAG 2.2 adds new success criteria (notably around focus indicators and dragging movements). While not yet legally mandated in most jurisdictions, it is best practice and will likely become the legal baseline over time. Consider planning for WCAG 2.2 AA compliance.
2. VPAT/ACR: For US government sales, prepare a Voluntary Product Accessibility Template (VPAT) or Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR) documenting your conformance with Section 508 / WCAG 2.1 AA.
3. Accessibility Statements: EU and UK public sector regulations require a published accessibility statement. This is recommended best practice for all customer-facing products.
4. WCAG 3.0: Still in development and not yet a legal requirement. Do not use WCAG 3.0 as your compliance baseline at this time.
